activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Article I, Section 7 of the US Constitution requires all bills for raising revenue to originate in the House of Representatives, though the Senate may amend them.
story:
The lasagna had gone cold at one corner of the table because nobody had touched it there; the plates had been shoved aside to make room for Ella's laptop, three textbooks, and the draft she'd printed at the library because she trusted paper more. The bill was hers, mostly. It would impose a small tax on disposable vape products and route the money to school counseling programs, and on Friday it had to survive the model Congress in the gymnasium, where Ms. Costa would preside as speaker and half the sophomore class would vote it down for sport.

"You can't introduce it yet," Skyler said, mouth full of garlic bread. "You said the Senate section meets first."

"Then I'll introduce it there," Ella said, reaching across Marie-Ange for the butter.

Marie-Ange caught her wrist, not hard, just enough to stop her. "You can't. It's a tax bill. Tax bills have to start in the House."

Ella pulled her hand free and laughed, the kind of laugh she regretted even while it was still in the air. "Says who?"

"Says the Constitution. Article One, Section Seven. All bills for raising revenue originate in the House." Marie-Ange turned her own notebook around so Ella could see the page, the clause copied out in her cramped handwriting, which Ella had always malign privately, calling it ransom-note script, though she'd never said it out loud where it could hurt. "The Senate can still amend them. It just can't start them."

The kitchen went quiet enough that they could hear the dishwasher's second rinse. Their father stood at the sink with his back to them, and Ella understood from the stillness of his shoulders that he was listening and would not rescue her. She scrolled to the pocket Constitution she'd downloaded in September, typed "revenue," and there it was, every word the way Marie-Ange had said it. Her draft had the Senate bill number at the top. Her beautiful preamble, the one Ms. Costa had called perspicacious in the margin last week, was attached to the wrong chamber.

"It's fine," Ella said. "I'll change the header."

"That's not the only thing," Marie-Ange said, and Ella felt the old suspicion rise, the one that said Marie-Ange hoarded rules the way other people hoarded gossip, waiting for the moment of maximum damage. "Your counseling programs are funded through the school board. The tax goes to the state. You'd need an appropriation clause or the whole thing is metonymy dressed up as policy. The bill isn't the funding, Ella. You're writing like it is."

She said it without heat, which was worse. Ella looked at the draft and saw that Marie-Ange had already marked the weak clause in pencil, last night probably, while they'd sat at this same table and Ella had talked for forty minutes about parliamentary procedure, about cloture, about everything except the sentence that didn't work. She had assumed the freelancing was a grab for credit. Now the pencil marks looked like somebody doing her a favor she hadn't asked for and didn't know how to thank her for.

"Okay," Ella said. "House it starts in. Senate amends. I'll write the appropriation clause tonight."

"You'll write it," Marie-Ange said. "I want to be listed as co-sponsor. First co-sponsor."

Ella's father turned around then, drying his hands slowly on the towel. Skyler reached for the cold corner of lasagna as if it were the most interesting thing in the room. Ella understood the trade being offered and understood, too, that she had misread everything until now: Marie-Ange had not been waiting to wound her, and that didn't make the demand smaller. The bill would carry both their names at the podium on Friday, and when Ms. Costa called it to order, the first voice the gymnasium heard explaining it would be Ella's, but the thing being explained would no longer be entirely hers.

"First co-sponsor," Ella said. "But I open the debate."

Marie-Ange considered this the way she considered everything, with her chin down and her eyes steady, and then she picked up the pencil, crossed out the Senate bill number at the top of the page, and wrote the House designation above it in her cramped, deliberate hand.

"Debate's yours," she said. "The committee hearing is mine."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: US employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit.
story:
The pay stub was smaller than the envelope it came in, and the envelope was smaller than Angelina had imagined all week at the registers, bagging cantaloupe and pretending not to hear when customers called her "sweetie." She had done the math on her break with a pen from the lost-and-found cup: nineteen hours at eleven dollars an hour. Two hundred and nine dollars. The check said one hundred ninety-five point nine three. She stood in the stockroom doorway holding both numbers in her head the way you hold water in your hands.

"That's not a rounding error," said Viviane, who worked the deli slicer and had opinions about everything except the things that mattered. "That's thirteen dollars. Thirteen dollars buys a lot of ham."

"Twelve, whatever." Angelina folded the stub along its perforation. Behind them, the freezer hummed like it was about to ionize the whole aisle, the air so dry and crackly that her hair had been misbehaving since October. Outside the loading dock window the sky had gone the gray-green color it got before hail, and she thought about her mother saying storms felt different when you had money in your pocket, or didn't.

Mika appeared with a cart of dented cans, breathing hard from the ramp. "Six point two percent," he said, before anyone had asked him anything. Mika read the employee handbook in the break room like other people read their phones. "I did the same math last month. You take your wages, they withhold six point two percent for Social Security, it comes right off the top."

"Off the top of eleven dollars an hour," Viviane said. "Off the top of my dreams."

Angelina did the arithmetic on the back of a receipt. Two hundred nine times point zero six two. Twelve dollars and ninety-six cents, and there it was, the missing money, accounted for to the penny. She felt something between relief and resentment, the two of them occupying the same chair. The relief won by a little. At least the world was subtracting from her on purpose.

"There's a limit, though," Mika added, pushing the cart onward. "It only goes up to a yearly wage limit. After that they stop taking it."

"At my rate," Viviane said, "I will reach that limit on approximately the twelfth of never."

Angelina taped the receipt inside her locker, next to the shift schedule Ms. Johansson posted every Sunday in her slanted, anachronistic handwriting, all loops and underlines, as if the schedule were a document from a century when people wrote things out carefully. Ms. Johansson had hired her on the spot two weeks ago, saying, "You look like someone who shows up," which Angelina had taken as the highest compliment available and still did, mostly.

She texted her mother from the bus stop, hail ticking against the plastic roof like a fingernail. Smaller than I thought. I figured out why though. Six point two for Social Security, only up to a yearly wage limit, so it could be worse. Her mother replied with a thumbs up and then, a minute later, a separate message: You learned that yourself? Angelina looked at the message for a while. It was true that Ms. Johansson had never explained it, that nobody had, that Mika had only confirmed what the numbers had already told her. It was also true that eleven dollars minus six point two percent was still eleven dollars minus six point two percent, however you found out. She typed "yes" and put the phone away, not sure which of those was the answer.

At home she sat at the kitchen table with her college savings jar, an actual glass jar, which Viviane had called "adorable" in a tone Angelina had chosen not to parse. She counted the check into it: one hundred ninety-five dollars and ninety-three cents, minus the ten she owed her brother for the bus pass, minus the four for the fries she and Mika had split after the shift, the salt still on her fingers. She had wanted this job to feel like a door opening. It felt more like a door opening onto a hallway with more doors, each one marked with a small fee.

Viviane texted a photo of her own paycheck with the caption "hostage situation." Mika texted a picture of a fjord he had apparently looked up on his break, blue water, black cliffs, some fantasy of a place wages couldn't reach. Angelina set the jar on her windowsill where the hail had stopped and the light was coming back, ordinary and sideways, and shook the jar until the bills settled.

"Grow," she told it.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
story:
The house smelled of tatami and mothballs, and every surface still held his grandfather's shape: the reading glasses folded on the armrest, the go board with a game unfinished, the slippers by the door turned toward the garden as though he had just stepped out. James had been there four days, and he still could not decide what he had come to do. His grandmother moved through the rooms like a stoic, thanking the neighbors who brought food, refilling the tea, never once weeping, and her steadiness felt to James like an accusation. He had spent three weeks with the man in his whole life. He was sixteen and he had let the last summer slip past with excuses about a job at Mr. Bennett's hardware store and a camping trip with Alvin, and now the only grandfather he had was a photograph on the butsudan, a small shrine his grandmother dusted each morning with the same cloth, the same motions.

He found the box on the second night, up in the closet where she told him extra fans were stored. Inside were letters, decades of them, aerograms and thin airmail envelopes, every one addressed to his grandmother in the same careful hand and opened so many times the creases had gone soft as cloth. James could not read them. Two years of Japanese at his school had underpinned nothing; he could pick out a word here and there, grandfather, summer, thank you, and the rest was a fence he could not get over. He sat cross-legged on the tatami with the box in his lap until his grandmother found him there, and she looked at the letters and then at him, and said, "He wrote every week, even after we stopped needing to." She did not translate them. She only said he could keep the box, and went back downstairs.

The next morning Finnley climbed over the low wall between the two properties, the way he apparently always had, a tall half-Japanese boy from Osaka who was spending the summer with his own grandmother and who had appointed himself James's guide without asking. James had told him almost nothing, but Finnley had a way of not needing telling. They sat on the porch eating the melon his grandmother cut for them, and James finally said it, the thing he could not say at the funeral or on the plane: that he wanted to say goodbye and did not know how, that all the ways he knew, a card, flowers, standing quietly at a graveside, felt borrowed and wrong.

Finnley set down his slice. "It's August," he said. "It's Obon." He said the word the way James's grandmother said it, with a small bow of the head. "At Obon the families light fires to welcome the spirits of the ancestors home. My grandmother has been cleaning the house for a week, for him." He pointed his chin at the garden next door, then at James's side of the wall. "And at the end, everyone floats lanterns down the river to guide the spirits back." He shrugged, as if to say, that's just what happens, and stole the last piece of melon.

The fire was small, mukaebi, Finnley's grandmother called it, lit at the gate in a shallow clay dish, and James watched the flames stand up in the wind and lean and stand again. His grandmother knelt beside it and said nothing, and James knelt too, and the smoke went up into the summer dark. All week after that the house filled, cousins and neighbors, drums from the temple in the evening, and on the last night the whole town walked down to the river carrying paper lanterns, each one with a name written down its face in wet black ink. His grandmother wrote the name herself, then held the brush out to James. His hand was not steady. The characters came out crooked, and he thought of the letters in the box, all that careful handwriting going one way across the ocean for fifty years while his own had gone nowhere at all.

He had assumed, walking down, that the lantern was a sending away, an ending, and that this would let him close the account. But when he crouched at the water's edge with the lantern and felt the current pull at it like something alive, he understood he had it half wrong. The fire at the gate had been a welcome, not a farewell; the lantern was the farewell, and only after the welcome. You could not have one without the other, and he had arrived trying to skip straight to the second. It was a tenable position, maybe, for people who had already said hello enough times. He was not one of them, and no single night on a river could make him one.

He set the lantern on the water anyway. It turned once, caught the current, and joined the slow procession of lights already moving downstream, hundreds of them, whole families of light going away together. His grandmother's hand rested briefly on his shoulder. Behind them Finnley was arguing with his grandmother about something, his voice bright and ordinary, and ahead the lantern with the crooked name grew smaller, and James stood there watching until he could not tell which light was his.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In the United States, the Department of Housing and Urban Development considers a household cost-burdened if it spends more than 30 percent of its income on housing.
story:
Christian spread the two leases across the library table like a man laying out cards he already distrusted. One was for a studio above the laundromat on Fifth Street, six hundred and fifty dollars a month plus utilities, which the landlord's fine print described as "tenant's responsibility, estimated." The other was a room in a shared house near campus, four hundred and ninety dollars with everything included, except that Joshua had texted him a photo of a ceiling stain the size of a dinner plate with the caption "the situation."

Joshua dropped into the chair opposite him, uninvited, holding a chocolate milk he had clearly purchased instead of lunch. "So you're doing it," he said. "You're actually moving out."

"I'm doing the math first." Christian had a legal pad, a calculator, and a pay stub from the grocery store where he worked twenty-four hours a week. He had learned, mostly through failure, to compartmentalize: schoolwork in one mental drawer, the future in another, and this, apparently, in a third drawer he'd only just discovered he owned.

"Estimate the utilities," Joshua said, leaning over the pad. "That's where they get you. My cousin paid like two hundred a month for heat one winter."

"Two hundred is high. Let's say ninety average for electric and water." Christian wrote it down and felt the studio slip away from him before the arithmetic was even finished: seven hundred and forty a month. His paycheque came to about sixteen hundred after taxes. He divided, and the number that came out was roughly forty-six percent.

"Forty-six percent of your income on housing," Joshua said slowly, reading it upside down. "That sounds made up. Like a statistic from a commercial."

"It's not made up." Christian pulled out his phone, because the number had bothered him in a way he couldn't name, a shape he felt he should recognize. He searched and found a page from the Department of Housing and Urban Development. "Here. In the United States, HUD considers a household cost-burdened if it spends more than thirty percent of its income on housing." He read the line twice, then said it aloud, quietly, as if testing the weight of it.

"So you'd be burdened."

"Cost-burdened. Technically." Christian turned back to the other lease. Four hundred and ninety, all in. He did the division again: just under thirty-one percent. Barely over. He sat back and looked at the two columns, one catastrophically over the line, one hovering a breath above it, and felt something equivocal settle over him, a hesitation between relief and the suspicion that a threshold you barely clear is not really a safety but a lucky bounce. He did not know, for instance, whether groceries counted, or the bus pass, or whether the estimate on utilities would hold, and no amount of arithmetic would tell him.

"Here's the thing," Joshua said, and Christian looked up, because Joshua's voice had gone careful, the way it did before he asked for something. "The room in the house. There's two openings. I was going to apply for the other one." He rotated his chocolate milk a quarter turn. "We could split the groceries. I'd get the stained ceiling room, obviously, I'm used to disappointment." He grinned, but his leg was bouncing under the table, and Christian understood that Joshua wanted this more than he was letting on, wanted an exit from his own house, where his father's rules operated, in Joshua's phrasing, purely as deterrence against anyone having a life.

"You didn't mention that part."

"You were doing your little pad thing. I didn't want to interrupt the science."

Christian laughed despite himself. He looked at the numbers again, at the forty-six and the thirty-one, at the ceiling stain Joshua had photographed like a crime scene, and he thought about how little he could actually predict. Maybe utilities would be sixty. Maybe the stain was a one-time leak. Maybe thirty-one percent would become thirty-four and he would be burdened in a way some government agency had defined for him before he had ever thought to define it himself. He only knew that one door was shut and the other was barely open, and barely open was still open.

He pulled out a pen and, on the back of the laundromat lease, wrote the landlord a short decline, dated it, and folded it in half. Joshua watched him do it with an expression he was trying and failing to keep neutral.

"So is that a yes to the house? Because I kind of already sent them my application. This morning. Before you did the math."

Christian stopped with the paper halfway into his bag. "You applied for a room in a house I hadn't chosen yet?"

"I applied for a room in a house you were obviously going to choose. Forty-six percent, man. Even I can do that math." Joshua raised the chocolate milk in a small toast. "So, roommates?"

Christian shook his head, still half-laughing, and pulled the house lease back across the table. He signed his name at the bottom of the application, then slid the pen toward Joshua.

"You're getting the stained ceiling room," he said.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The GED tests were created in 1942 to let military service members and veterans who had not finished high school show high-school-level skills.
story:
The gown arrived folded in a plastic sleeve, and Eva carried it upstairs like something that might bruise. Her mother had cleared the hall closet that morning, and three cardboard boxes now sat on Eva's bed, their flaps open, exhaling dust. She was supposed to be sorting them for the move after graduation, deciding what deserved the truck ride to the new apartment and what did not. Instead she stood in front of the boxes in her socks, holding the gown, not yet ready to hang it.

The second box held her grandfather's things. She knew his handwriting from birthday cards, the careful slanted letters, and there was a lot of it here: ration booklets, a photograph of young men squinting on a dock, a folded flag she left folded. Near the bottom, in a yellowed envelope, she found a certificate with a gold seal. It looked important, the kind of document a school might frame and valorize in a hallway display, and for a moment she thought it was a diploma. Then she read the words across the top and frowned.

"What's a GED?" she asked that evening, when her grandfather came for dinner, which he did every Thursday now that her grandmother was gone. He was slow on the stairs and he always brought grapes even though nobody wanted them, and he took the envelope from her with both hands, the way people handle eggs.

"They made the tests in 1942," he said. "For service members and veterans who hadn't finished high school. So they could show high-school-level skills." He turned the certificate over, though the back was blank. "I got mine after I came back. Your grandmother got hers the regular way. She liked to say she finished and I only proved it."

Eeva laughed, then caught herself, unsure whether it was a joke he wanted laughed at. Her mother called from the kitchen that dinner was ready, and Rayyan texted twice about the graduation party, and Darius had sent a photo of his own gown hanging crooked on a closet door with the caption, am I supposed to feel different. She hadn't answered any of it yet.

Later, at the table, she watched her grandfather spoon the soup her mother had made because it was easy on his teeth, and she thought about the ceremony on Saturday, about walking across a stage in the gown that still smelled like plastic. At school they had been told all year that this was an achievement, and she had believed it, mostly, except on mornings when it felt more like an exit. Darius had a scholarship to a school nine hours away. Rayyan was staying home and saving money and refused to be ashamed of it, though people kept trying. Eva herself had deferred for a year and told everyone it was for the internship, which was partly true and partly fear, and she had not yet decided how much of each.

"Does it bother you?" she asked her grandfather, when her mother had gone to find the good bread. "That you didn't get the real one?"

He considered the question longer than she expected. "The tests were hard," he said finally. "Nobody gave us amnesty for wrong answers." He tore his bread in half and put one half on her plate, an old habit from feeding four children. "Your grandmother finished in 1950 and I tested in 1946 and we ended up in the same house, same jobs, same arguments. I used to think the paper made the difference. Now I think I was being grandiose about paper."

Eva turned her spoon in the bowl. She wanted to ask whether that was true or just a comfortable thing to say at eighty-six, whether proving something and finishing something really landed in the same house, whether her own year off was the beginning of a different road or just a longer way to the same place. He was watching her, though, with the patient look of a man who had waited out artillery, so she asked something smaller instead.

"Can I keep the certificate? For the apartment."

"You can keep the whole box if you haul it yourself." He pushed back his chair and went to the window, where the streetlight was coming on, and stood there with his hands behind his back like a man reviewing a diminished parade. Eva slid the envelope under the sleeve of her folded gown, where it made a small stiff ridge in the plastic. Then she texted Darius back: no, you're not supposed to feel different, and then, before she could delete it, bring the good speaker Saturday.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In the United States, the House of Representatives impeaches a president by a simple majority, but the Senate needs a two-thirds vote to convict and remove them.
story:
The folding chairs in the town hall basement had been arranged in a horseshoe, and Michael took the one nearest the radiator because the room was cold in the way of rooms that smell of coffee and mimeograph ink. He had come for extra credit, which Ms. Littlechild had offered to anyone attending the public forum on the county's new youth council, and he had come also because Austyn had texted him three exclamation points about it, which for Austyn amounted to a manifesto. What Michael had not expected was that the moderator, a retired parliamentarian named only as the moderator, would open the floor by asking the few teenagers present to demonstrate, live and unrehearsed, how a government actually falls.

"Who can tell me," she said, holding her gavel like a baton, "how a prime minister loses office in a country like ours versus how a president loses it in the United States?"

Taylor raised her hand first, which surprised no one. "In a parliamentary system the parliament can just vote no confidence and the government's out," she said. "Like, the head of government is basically an employee of the legislature. The president isn't. You have to impeach him."

"Impeach," said a man near the back, one of the pensioners who came to every meeting and heckled only gently, "and there he goes."

"No," Michael said, before he had fully decided to speak. The word had come out of him the way words did when he was certain, and he was certain because he had written a paper on it in tenth grade, or half of one, the half he'd finished at midnight. "Impeachment removes the president."

The moderator did not correct him. She looked at him with a patience that felt, to Michael, like a hand hovering over a switch. "Does it," she said. "Would anyone like to test that against the record?"

Austyn, sitting two seats down with his hoodie pulled up like armor, leaned toward Michael and muttered, "I think you're about to be the demonstration."

The moderator beckoned them both to the front, and what followed was the strange pageant of a town hall turning itself into a classroom. She handed Michael and Austyn index cards, assigned roles, and had the horseshoe act as a legislature while she read from a dog-eared copy of a civics sourcebook she kept in her tote. Austyn, as the House, voted to impeach by a show of hands, a simple majority, hands up, hands down, done. Then the room became the Senate, and she asked for two-thirds, and the count fell short, and the pretend president, a bewildered woman from the county extension office, remained in office.

"So," the moderator said, "impeachment is the accusation. Removal is the conviction. In the United States, the House of Representatives impeaches a president by a simple majority, but the Senate needs a two-thirds vote to convict and remove them."

Michael stood there with his index card going soft in his hand. He thought of the paper he'd written, the grade on it, a fat red A circled at the top by a teacher who apparently had not read the paragraph where he'd claimed, with the confidence of the sleep-deprived, that impeachment itself was removal. He had never gone back to check. It was a small thing, a wrong word, and yet it had sat in a drawer in his house for two years being wrong, and he had gone on thinking of himself as someone who understood this stuff.

During the break, when the room loosened into clusters around the coffee urn, Taylor found him by the folding table with the day-old donuts. "That was brutal," she said, but not unkindly. "You okay?"

"I wrote a whole paper on it," Michael said. "Wrong in the middle of it. Nobody caught it."

"That's the part I'd hate," Taylor said. She bit a donut. "Not being wrong. Nobody noticing you were wrong. What's the point of turning something in if it just comes back with a grade and nobody actually reads your thinking?"

Michael turned his cup of coffee without drinking it. He had been trying lately to introspect less, on the theory that he spent too much time examining his own motives and not enough acting on them, and here was the habit catching him anyway, taking out the memory and holding it to the light. The parliamentary system was parsimonious, he thought: one vote, one chamber, government falls, no drama. The presidential system spent more, demanded more, a majority here and a supermajority there, and what it bought with all that friction was a chief executive who could limp on, impeached but not removed, wounded but standing. Whether that was stability or paralysis depended, he supposed, on whether you trusted the man in the office.

The second half of the forum was a shouted argument about the youth council's budget, and the moderator let it run because, she said, "This is what a legislature sounds like before it learns procedure." A man in a windbreaker claimed the county should be run like a business, or better, by experts, by engineers and accountants, a kind of technocracy, and Ms. Littlechild, who had been silent in the third row for two hours, stood up and said, "The last time this county was run by experts alone, they closed two schools to save money and called it efficiency," and the room broke into applause and boos in almost equal measure.

Michael watched the moderator hold her gavel and not use it. She let the noise crest and fall on its own, the way tide does, and when the room finally quieted she said only, "Observe. This is a no-confidence vote in the making. Or it's nothing. You won't know which until someone actually calls the question."

Afterward, in the parking lot under the one working streetlight, Austyn pulled his hoodie down and said, "So did you learn anything, or did you just get publicly executed?"

"Both," Michael said. He still had the index card in his jacket pocket, the one with HOUSE written on it in the moderator's slanted hand, and he took it out and looked at it under the light. Austyn started the car and honked once.

"You keeping that?" Austyn called through the window.

Michael folded the card in half and put it back in his pocket, then opened the door and got in.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
The robotics room smelled of flux and cold pizza, and the drive base sat between them on the bench like a patient nobody wanted to diagnose. Maxime had been captain for three weeks, and in those three weeks he had learned to run a meeting, to order parts, and to say "good job, everyone" with a conviction he did not feel. The thing he had not learned was the thing now required of him: Louis's code had a reversed sign in the gyroscope correction, and the robot had driven itself into the wall four times that afternoon, and Louis did not know why.

"Maybe the motor's dying," Louis said, unscrewing the casing again. His hands were steady, his voice slightly querulous, as if the robot were being unfair to him on purpose. Rosemarie, who had found the sign error in the log files twenty minutes ago, said nothing. She caught Maxime's eye and then looked back at her laptop, typing with the deliberate calm of someone waiting out a storm.

Maxime said nothing too, and that was the problem. He had read something two nights ago, late, in an essay Ms. Katz had left on the resource page for their group dynamics unit, a passage about a researcher named Amy Edmondson who in 1999 described what she called psychological safety, a team's shared belief that it was safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake. He had circled the phrase twice. It had sounded like something from a poster in a guidance office, but it stayed with him, the way certain words do, and now the room was demonstrating its absence with the precision of a lab experiment. Everyone knew. Nobody spoke. The silence was not kindness; it was insurance.

He tried a small experiment first, to forestall the harder conversation. "Rosemarie, anything in the logs?" She hesitated, then read out the numbers, careful and neutral, and Louis nodded along without hearing them, already reaching for the multimeter. Data was safe; it carried no judgment. But the data was not the point, and Maxime understood, with a small cold clarity, that if he let the afternoon end this way, Louis would go home believing the robot was broken rather than the code, and next week Louis would hide his work, and the week after that Rosemarie would stop checking the logs at all. Beliefs like that spread through a team the way moisture spreads through the substrate of a circuit board, invisibly, until everything corrodes.

So that night he wrote a message, because saying it in the room felt like ambush and saying it never felt like cowardice he could live with. He drafted it four times on his phone, the cursor blinking in the dark of his bedroom.

Louis. It's not the motor. Rosemarie found it in the logs. There's a reversed sign in the gyro correction, around line 40 of your drive loop. It's a small thing and it's buried in a section nobody else could have written, which is why we didn't catch it sooner. I should have told you at the bench instead of making you hear it from a text. Come early tomorrow and we'll fix it together before anyone else arrives.

He read it over, deleted "which is why we didn't catch it sooner" because it smelled of flattery, and put it back because it happened to also be true. He pressed send before he could refine it into nothing.

Louis was already there in the morning, the program open on his screen, his finger resting on the offending line. He did not look up when Maxime came in. "You're right," he said. "It's backwards. I flipped it when I refactored." A pause. "It was there for two weeks." Maxime pulled a chair over beside him rather than across from him, which felt like a decision worth making, and they traced the logic together, and when the correction was in and the robot rolled straight down the hallway for the first time all week, Louis laughed once, short and surprised, and said, "So we wasted a whole afternoon on multimeter readings." "We wasted it," Maxime said, "because I didn't tell you what I knew. That part was mine."

Rosemarie arrived with two bagels and no comment about the logs, but at the next build session, when her own code froze the arm mid-lift, she said "I broke something, come look" before anyone could ask, and the words came out easy, ordinary, like reporting the temperature. Maxime noticed it the way you notice a door that used to stick and now doesn't. He could not have proven the connection, and he was honest with himself about that; maybe Rosemarie would have said it anyway, maybe the team had only needed a good afternoon. He only knew that this week, when Louis handed him the new drive code to review, he said, "Your comments are better than mine, but you still bury your variables, section three, the ones with the lowercase L's that look like ones," and Louis grinned and said, "Noted," and opened the file.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under the US Federal Trade Commission's Cooling-Off Rule, buyers can cancel certain sales made at home or at temporary locations until midnight of the third business day after the sale.
story:
The gym was quiet on weekday mornings, which was why Samuel liked the shift. He stamped renewal forms, checked IDs against the liability waiver on file, and once an hour wiped down the front desk with a rag that smelled of lemon and chlorine. His mother had always said he was too young for a job that involved signatures, and he had pointed out that at eighteen he had signed the employment contract himself, initialing each page of terms and conditions while Mr. Gauthier, the owner, watched with an expression of mild impatience, as though consent were a formality everyone should hurry through.

That Saturday she came back from a wedding expo at the Marriott with a folder. Inside the folder was a two-year membership to Samuel's own gym, sold at a booth between the cake samples and the photo booth, three hundred and forty dollars paid on the spot. She had signed it while a man in a fitted blazer talked about commitment. By Sunday morning she regretted it the way she regretted the one time she had dyed her hair, quietly and completely, and she slid the folder across the kitchen table without a word.

"I can look at it," Samuel said, though he already had, the night before, reading the terms twice while his phone fermented in his pocket with texts from Vera about a party he wasn't going to. The contract said nothing about cancelling. Nothing about anything, really, except fees. He knew the gym's own in-house memberships could be cancelled with thirty days' notice, but this one had come through a vendor, some company called VitalFit, and the paperwork had a hotel's address printed at the top.

On Monday he asked Vera, who sat behind the desk doing homework and eating a protein bar in microscopic bites. "If someone sells you something at a booth," he said, "a hotel booth, not here, are you stuck?"

"Ask Giulia," Vera said. "Her whole family is lawyers."

Giulia wasn't working until Thursday, but she texted him back a screenshot from the FTC website with one line circled in red, and after that Samuel read the page himself three times, because a circled screenshot was not a source he was willing to cite to Mr. Gauthier. The rule had a name, the Cooling-Off Rule, and the page said buyers could cancel certain sales made at home or at temporary locations until midnight of the third business day after the sale. His mother had signed on Saturday. He counted on his fingers, feeling like a child, and then counted again to be sure the counting itself wasn't the error. Monday was day three.

He brought the folder to work. At lunch he typed the cancellation letter on the gym's ancient office computer, dated it, and had his mother's signature photocopied beside her printed name, since the rule seemed to want the notice in writing. Mr. Gauthier found him at the fax machine, which no one had used since Samuel was hired and which he had operated with the pedantry of a museum docent, reading the manual first.

"That's not our contract," Mr. Gauthier said, taking the folder. "VitalFit rents our floor. They're capricious about paperwork. Some months they honor cancellations, some months they claim they never received them."

"Then I'll fax it and mail it and keep copies," Samuel said. "It's their rule as much as anyone's. Federal." He said the word and then, feeling the weight of it, said the rest. "They have until midnight of the third business day, under the Cooling-Off Rule. It's on the FTC site. My mom signed at a temporary location."

Mr. Gauthier looked at him for a long moment, then at the fax machine, which was screaming a page into the void. "You counted the business days correctly? Saturday doesn't count."

"Monday's the third. I counted twice."

"Count a third time when you get home," Mr. Gauthier said, but he was smiling in the way he smiled at members who argued about the fine print and turned out to be right. He set the folder on the desk. "You realize you just spent your lunch break doing this for free."

Vera leaned over from the other side of the desk, holding out the last inch of her protein bar as a ceremonial offering. Samuel took it, faxed the second copy, and put the original in his backpack, zipping the pocket shut over his mother's name.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: An authentic cadence, a V chord moving to the I chord, sounds final, which is why melodies usually end their last phrase with it.
story:
The rehearsal room behind the concert hall smelled of dust and old velvet, and Victoria had claimed the piano in the corner by arriving forty minutes early, which she considered a legitimate act of war. On the music stand sat her manuscript paper: sixteen bars, four phrases, chord symbols penciled above every measure with the optimism of someone who had only learned the symbols two weeks ago. The youth composition showcase was in three days, and her melody still refused to end.

"It's like a sentence with no period," said Alivia, dropping her bag on the floor and leaning over Victoria's shoulder. "You keep stopping, but nothing finishes."

"That's very wise," Victoria said. "Did you write that on the bus?"

"I did, actually. I collect epigrams now. It's my new thing." Alivia tapped the last two measures. "Play it again."

Victoria played it again. The melody climbed through the first phrase, wandered in the second, tightened in the third, and then arrived at the final bar and simply stopped, like someone turning off a light mid-thought. Alivia winced theatrically, which was unkind but accurate.

Veronica arrived late, as constitutionally required, holding a coffee she had clearly been carrying since another borough. She was the one who had taken theory the longest, and Victoria had been rationing her questions all week so as not to use her up entirely. "Okay," Veronica said, sitting on the piano bench's far edge, "play the last phrase but stay on the five chord. G, then C. Just try it."

Victoria tried it. The final note of the melody sat on the G chord for a beat, then dropped to the C chord underneath, and the room, which had been holding its breath for two weeks, exhaled. All three of them heard it at once. It sounded finished. It sounded like a door closing gently and completely.

"What was that?" Victoria asked, her pencil already moving.

"Authentic cadence," Veronica said. "Five chord to the one chord. That's why melodies end their last phrase with it. It sounds final." She sipped her ancient coffee with total serenity, a prophet of the commonsense.

Victoria wrote the chord change in, then sat back and glared at the page, because it had introduced a new problem. Her third phrase ended on the same V-to-I motion, and now that she could hear it, the ending arrived twice, like a guest saying goodbye in the hallway and then again at the car. The cadence that emancipated her final bar had quietly imprisoned her ninth. She crossed out the D minor under bar eight, tried an F, hated it, tried A minor, and found that the melody now lingered there instead of resolving, which was, she admitted to Alivia, exactly what she wanted the middle of the piece to do: hesitate.

"So the trick," Victoria said slowly, "is to save it. Spend the final-sounding thing once, at the end, and make everything else sound like it's still deciding."

"That's an epigram too," Alivia said. "I'm taking it. I'm destitute of epigrams compared to you two."

"You cannot be destitute of epigrams, that's not a real condition," said Veronica, and Victoria laughed and played the whole sixteen bars through, start to finish, for the first time with the ending that ended. The hesitation in the middle now sounded deliberate rather than lost, and she could not decide whether that was true or whether she had merely said it enough times to make it true, and she decided she could live without deciding.

Ms. Morningstar put her head in the door ten minutes before the showcase rehearsal was to begin, surveyed the manuscript, the crossed-out chords, and the three of them crowded around one bench like people sharing a small fire, and said only, "Bar twelve, dear, your soprano E clashes with the C in the left hand. Or keep it, if that's the point." Then she was gone down the corridor.

Victoria looked at bar twelve. She looked at Alivia, who shrugged with magnificent uselessness, and at Veronica, who was already reaching past her to press the key.

"Play it," Veronica said.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
story:
Wyatt kept telling people he was fine, and the strange thing was that he half believed it, the way you can believe a weather forecast for a city you never visit. He stood in his grandfather's kitchen on the morning after the funeral, holding a mug of coffee he had no intention of drinking, and told his mother for the third time that he'd rather stay at the house alone than drive back with the relatives. She looked at him the way she looked at the radiator that clicked but never warmed, and let him stay.

The house smelled like pipe smoke that had soaked into the curtains decades ago. His grandfather had died in the upstairs bedroom, though nobody said that part out loud; they said he passed, they said he went peacefully, as if death were a courteous guest. Wyatt ran a finger along the windowsill where they used to line up dominoes, his grandfather setting them up in long winding routes while Wyatt, a neophyte at six, knocked them over too early every single time. He could still hear the old man laughing about it, refusing to be annoyed, saying patience was a thing you grew into like a coat.

His phone buzzed. Haroon had sent a photo from the movie theatre two towns over, the marquee showing some action sequel they'd been talking about for months. We're going at 7, Delilah's in. You in? Wyatt typed no, deleted it, typed maybe, deleted that too. The funeral had been four days ago. He set the phone face down on the counter as if it were something hot.

He spent the afternoon doing what he called helping, which was mostly opening drawers and not knowing what to do with what he found. In the study, behind a stack of woodworking magazines, there was a paperback with a cracked spine: a psychology text, second-hand, a receipt from a university bookstore tucked inside dated from years before Wyatt was born. His grandfather had taken a counseling course after his own father died; Wyatt's mother had mentioned it once, briefly, the way she mentioned most hard things. He sat on the floor and started paging through it, mostly to avoid the relatives downstairs arguing about who got the cedar chest.

There was a chapter with a diagram: two circles, side by side, arrows looping between them. One circle said confronting, the other said restoring. Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model, the caption read, describing grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction toward some finish line. Wyatt read it twice. His grandfather had underlined a single sentence in pencil: not a line you cross, a door you keep walking through, both ways. The handwriting was shaky, smaller than the notes in the margins of the woodworking magazines, and Wyatt had to put the book down on his knees for a minute.

He texted Haroon: is the 7 o'clock still happening. Haroon replied within seconds, then called. "You sure? You don't have to be a monk about it," Haroon said. Wyatt said he was sure, or sure enough. "That diagram in your grandpa's book," he said. "It's the dual process model. Back and forth, not through." There was a pause on the line, and then Haroon said, "Okay. Save me a seat on the other side of the popcorn." Wyatt said he'd try, and for the first time all week that didn't feel like a lie he was telling to make things easier for other people.

Delilah picked him up at quarter to seven because his mother had taken the car. On the drive she talked about her summer job and a professor she'd already emailed, and Wyatt listened, and somewhere in the middle of it he laughed at something she said, really laughed, and then felt the guilt arrive like a bill collector. He waited for her to look at him sideways. She didn't. She just kept driving, one hand on the wheel, streetlights sliding across her face.

The movie was loud and ridiculous and he enjoyed it without reservation for maybe forty minutes, and then a grandfather character appeared on screen doing a crossword, and Wyatt went under for a while, sitting in the dark with his throat working, and nobody around him knew. Afterward, in the parking lot, Haroon asked if it was good. "Mostly," Wyatt said. "There was a part in the middle I missed." Haroon nodded like that was a normal thing to say about a movie, which, Wyatt was beginning to understand, it was.

Driving back through the dark, he thought about his grandfather pencilling that note to himself, some years and some griefs ago, trying to cauterize the fear that going to a film or laughing at dinner meant betraying the dead, and deciding instead that it didn't. It was a parsimonious theory, Wyatt thought, two circles and some arrows, no ceremony to it, and yet it fit better than anything anyone had said at the funeral. He didn't know if he believed it all the way through. He didn't know if the house would feel the same when they sold it, or if he'd keep finding the book in drawers for the rest of his life, or whether his grandfather had ever finished reading it. Delilah pulled up outside and left the engine running. Wyatt sat with his hand on the door. "Can we drive past the old house once more before you drop me at my mom's?"

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of an image, and artists often draw that space to get a shape's outline right.
story:
Raphael would tell you, if you asked, that he was the best artist in his grade, and he would almost believe it. The evidence was thin: one watercolor of a heron that his mother had framed, and a reputation built mostly on being the only kid who carried a sketchbook everywhere. What he would not mention, unless pressed, was the chair.

The chair was the problem. The public library was holding a contest, entries due Friday, and Raphael had decided on a still life: the old wooden chair by the window, the one with the wobbled spindle, drawn in charcoal. He had spent two afternoons at the library failing at it. Every chair he drew looked like a fence pretending to be furniture. He had blamed the charcoal, the light, the paper. He had not yet blamed Raphael.

He spread his supplies across the long table near the periodicals, which was where Annabelle found him.

"You look like the library lambasted you," she said, dropping her bag. "What is that, a dog cage?"

"It's a chair."

"Oh, is it?" She tilted her head. "I thought it might be modern. Like, a statement."

Annabelle had entered the contest too, a collage of the town's four traffic circles, and she was so relaxed about it that Raphael suspected she would win. Her phone buzzed and she read a message from Macey out loud, holding it up like evidence:

"Dear losers at the library. I have finished my entry, which is a painting of my cat, and it took me forty minutes. Raphael, my mum says hi and also that you left your hoodies at our house, plural, three hoodies. If you keep drawing that chair I will come over and draw it for you. Warm regards, Macey."

"Delete that," Raphael said.

"She typed it. It exists forever." Annabelle put the phone down. "Why is the chair so hard, though? It's just a chair. You draw herons."

"Herons don't have legs going every direction. And when I draw the legs, they're wrong, and then the seat's wrong, and it's like the chair is made of wrongness."

Annabelle pulled the chair from the window over to the table and sat in it, which Raphael felt was an act of provocation. "So draw me," she said. "I'm sitting in it. I'm very still."

He tried. He drew Annabelle, who kept giggling, and the chair under her came out worse than before, as if her sitting in it had offended it. He tore the sheet off, crumpled it, and added it to the small defeated mountain beside his elbow.

"I'm going to be a disaffected youth," he announced. "I'm going to stand outside the library and be disaffected about chairs."

"You'd need a hoodie," Annabelle said. "Oh wait, Macey has all your hoodies."

He laughed despite himself, and then, because he was avoiding the chair, he started doodling the window itself, and something odd happened. He drew the window frame, and the panes, and in charcoal he shaded the spaces around the chair's silhouette, where the light came through between the legs and around the seat, the gaps and the emptiness, and when he stepped back, the chair was there. Not drawn. Left over. The shape had appeared out of what he hadn't drawn, sharp and correct, sitting in the drawing like a fact.

"Annabelle. Look."

She leaned over. "How did you do that? You didn't even draw the chair."

"I drew everything that isn't the chair." He was flipping through one of the art books he'd pulled off the shelf an hour earlier, looking for anything, and there it was in a caption, the phrase he needed: negative space. "It's called negative space," he said, reading. "The empty area around and between the subjects of an image. Artists draw that space to get a shape's outline right."

"Drawing nothing to get something," Annabelle said. "That's like, a beautiful oxymoron. I'm putting that in my artist statement. Not the chair part. Just the beautiful part."

He started again on fresh paper, and this time he drew the gaps first: the triangles of light between the legs, the hole in the backrest, the air around the spindles. The chair emerged like it had been waiting. It was the best thing he had ever made, and it had taken him nine minutes after two days of failure, which was either a lesson or a joke, and he could not decide which.

Mr. Perera, the librarian, drifted past on his rounds and stopped. He looked for a long moment. "Is that the window chair?"

"Yes," Raphael said.

"Huh." Mr. Perera adjusted his glasses. "We're getting rid of that chair next month. Broken spindle. You should put the date on the drawing somewhere." He wandered off toward the front desk, and Raphael sat looking at what he had made, at the chair built out of emptiness, and understood that in a month it would be more real than the original. Whether the contest judges cared, whether Macey's cat won, whether drawing nothing counted as drawing something at all, he honestly did not know. He sharpened his charcoal and started on a second one, slower this time, leaving more room for the air.

Later his phone buzzed. Macey again: "Did you finish the chair? Annabelle says you drew the spaces between. Explain. Send picture. Not of your face, of the chair."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Encapsulation means hiding a class's data behind methods, so other code can use the object without depending on how it stores its data.
story:
The lab smelled of whiteboard marker and the radiator's burnt dust, and Arianna had typed the word "private" eleven times without believing it once. Coding club met on Thursdays in Room 114, where Ms. Kaur left the good chairs and pretended not to notice when someone ate a whole bag of chips at the back table. Arianna had her laptop open to a class called Student, three fields deep, and beside it a worksheet that said, in Ms. Kaur's looping hand, "Make the fields private. Write getters. Test."

"Test with what," Mehdi said, sliding his chair over. He had finished early, which he always did, and which he tried to make look like an accident. "You need someone to actually use your class, or the test means nothing."

"That's the part I don't get." She angled her screen toward him anyway. "If everything's private, how does anyone touch it?"

"That's the whole point." He tapped the worksheet. "Encapsulation. Ms. Kaur says it like it's a law of nature."

Arianna wrote the word in the margin of her notebook and, underneath it, a question mark she didn't show him. She built the class the way the sheet demanded: name as a String, gradeLevel as an int, both private, both wearing getters like stiff little uniforms. Then she wrote a runner that created a Student, called getName, printed it. Fine. It worked. She still felt like she'd followed a recipe without tasting the food.

What she wanted, and hadn't told anyone, was to submit this to the district's app contest, a study-buddy program where her class would hold everyone's profiles. The deadline was Sunday. And what she was afraid of, also unspoken, was that she'd build the whole thing and then want to change something small, some field, and watch the program crack down the middle the way her history project had last spring when she'd switched note-taking apps halfway through. She was sixteen and had already learned, from cheaper materials, that the way you store a thing and the way people use it get tangled if you let them.

Ally arrived late, hair still damp from swim practice, and dropped into the seat on Arianna's other side. "Can I use your Student class for my club sign-up sheet?" Ally asked. "Mine's a mess. Yours has, like, actual structure." Arianna said yes before she'd fully decided, and Ally copied the file, wrote her sign-up code against it, called getName and getGradeLevel the way the worksheet had, and printed forty labels for the bake sale by 4:15.

Then came the moment Arianna would later describe as the twist, though at the time it felt like tripping on a stair that wasn't there. She decided gradeLevel should be a double, because the middle schoolers got tracked into 7.5 and she was tired of fudging it. She changed the field from int to double, braced herself, and rebuilt everything, hers and Ally's and the label printer's worth of code. Nothing broke. Not one line. Ally's code had never once reached into the field; it had only ever knocked on the method doors. Arianna sat with her hands off the keyboard for a second, then changed the field back and forth twice more, just to watch nothing break again. It was as if she'd rebuilt the shelves behind a shop counter overnight and the customers never knew, because all they'd ever done was ask the person at the register.

"Wait," Mehdi said, watching her flip the type a third time. "Ally's code still runs?" He leaned across her to check. "That's it. That's what the sheet is for. Other code can use your object without depending on how it stores its data. I read that sentence four times last night and it meant nothing." He said it half annoyed, half delighted, the way he did when someone else's hands understood what his eyes hadn't.

Arianna started a new file, a version of Student that would let her parametrize the constructor, taking name and grade together, so she could stamp out profiles for the contest without copying and pasting. The recalcitrant part was the contest rubric itself, a PDF that refused to copy its text and had to be retyped by hand, and she was halfway through dragging its stubborn lines into her notes when Ally leaned over her shoulder.

"Hey," Ally said. "Since your class survived me, want to be my partner for the sign-up app instead of the contest thing? Less glory, more cookies." Arianna looked at the retyped rubric, at her clean little class with its private fields, at Ally's damp ponytail dripping a slow dark comma onto the desk. She could do both, probably. She could do neither. What she knew for sure was smaller than either choice: that hiding the data had protected it, and that the protection had turned out to be for Ally, who hadn't even known she was being protected, which felt like the strangest kind of kindness, the kind you build on purpose so nobody ever has to say thank you.

She saved the file, then closed the laptop halfway, folding the screen down like a lid over something still warm.

"Two cookies minimum," she said.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Using 2007 survey data, the US Census Bureau estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime.
story:
The moving truck pulled out of the cul-de-sac at nine in the morning, and Isla's father followed it in the family car with the last boxes wedged around her like luggage in a ship's hold. The keys to the old house had to be in the realtor's hands by five, which meant the truck could not stop for longer than lunch, which meant Isla had said goodbye to Ryleigh and Caitlyn at seven-thirty in the driveway, in the flat gray light, and had hated every second of how formal it had felt.

"Did you know," her father said, somewhere past the county line, "that using 2007 survey data, the US Census Bureau estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime?"

Isla looked up from her phone, where Ryleigh's last text sat unanswered. "Eleven point seven."

"Point seven," he confirmed. "You can't move point seven times, but that's the estimate. You're on number four, I think."

She did the arithmetic anyway, because she was the kind of person who couldn't leave a number alone: the apartment when she was two, the rental when she was six, this house since she was nine. Three, not four. She said so, and he conceded the point with a shrug that meant he had been aggrandizing their wandering, as he tended to, turning an ordinary shuffling between leases into something that sounded like a larger life.

They stopped for lunch at a diner off the highway, and while they ate, the twist arrived in the form of a text from Caitlyn: a photo of the diner's sign, taken from the parking lot, followed by the message "turn around." Isla went out through the door without quite deciding to. Ryleigh was leaning against Caitlyn's mother's car with two milkshakes going soft in the cupholders, and Caitlyn was holding a shoebox wrapped in tape, and they had driven forty minutes on a guess based on Isla's earlier complaint that her father always stopped at the same diner, the one with the subterranean basement level where they'd eaten once during a flood scare and she'd never stopped talking about it since.

"The box is the thing," Caitlyn said, pressing it into Isla's hands. "Everything from your locker. We broke into it. Legally. The janitor let us."

Inside were the small artifacts of three years: a debated history test on which Mr. Desir had written "an autodidact in the making, argue with me more," a folded program from the play they'd all crewed, a strip of photo-booth pictures. Isla had assumed she would find the rest of this in the new town, somehow, and had not examined the assumption until the shoebox made her hold it in her hands.

Her father came out, checked his watch, said five o'clock didn't move. They stood in the lot for six minutes. Ryleigh said they'd visit in October, and Isla heard the sentence as both a promise and a probability, and could not separate the two, and did not insult either of them by trying. She told them the number her father had told her, the whole thing, survey data and all, and Ryleigh laughed and said, "So this is, what, a ninth of your life's moving."

"Eleven point seven total," Isla said. "So not even a twelfth."

"But if the average is 11.7," Caitlyn said slowly, "some people move twenty times. And some move once." That had not occurred to Isla, and she stood there in the hot lot rearranging the fact in her head, because she had been treating the number as a sentence and it was more like a distribution, a spread of lives, and she could not yet know which kind of life was hers. She had two framings now and no verdict, and she found, to her surprise, that she could carry both without dropping either.

The car and the truck were on the interstate again by one. The shoebox rode on her lap. Her father drove steadily, checking the mirrors for the truck, watching the clock more than the road, and when her phone buzzed with a photo from Ryleigh, the three milkshake cups arranged like a still life on the dashboard of the departing car, Isla turned the screen toward her father without a word.

He glanced over, then back at the road. "October," he said.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The molar mass of a compound is the sum of the molar masses of the atoms in its formula; for carbon dioxide it is 12.01 plus two times 16.00, or 44.01 grams per mole.
story:
The kitchen table at his grandfather's house still had the plastic runner down the middle, and Cameron spread his chemistry worksheet on top of it while the kettle ticked behind him. The retake was Monday morning, eight a.m., and Ms. Saleh had underlined his error in red twice, which was twice more than she underlined anything. He had four days.

Jade had texted him the practice problems from her cabin, no signal after six, so this was it: him, the table, and a question that read, "How many moles of carbon dioxide form from 132 grams of the reactant, assuming complete conversion?" He copied it onto loose leaf and started the way he thought he was supposed to. Molar mass. Carbon, 12.01. Oxygen, 16.00. Add them, get 28.01, divide, done. He wrote 132 divided by 28.01 and got a number with too many decimals to feel right.

He called Karma, who picked up on the second ring and was clearly eating something. "You're doing it again," Karma said before Cameron had finished the problem. "Doing what." "The thing where you rush the setup because the arithmetic is the part you like." There was a silence on the line that Cameron filled by tapping his pencil against the table. He did not want setup advice. He wanted the answer, and he wanted it fast, because speed had been the whole point of him in every class since middle school. Fast was how he'd gotten the 61 in the first place.

"I have to go," Karma said. "Text me what you get." The line clicked off, which Karma could do, abruptly, without it meaning anything. Cameron sat back. His grandfather came through with two mugs and set one down on the far corner of the worksheet, careful, like it was a chess piece being placed.

"How's the schoolwork," his grandfather said, not exactly a question. Cameron said it was chemistry and it was fine. His grandfather pulled out the other chair and lowered himself into it. "I was canny with numbers," he said. "Forty years on the railway. You learn not to guess with freight." He didn't offer to help. He just drank his tea and read the funerals column of the local paper, which around here passed for oratory.

Cameron looked at his 28.01. Something about it bothered him the way a picture hung crooked bothers you before you can say why. He drew the molecule on the margin, one C, then two O's, both of them, side by side, because that was what carbon dioxide was, and he stopped. Two oxygens. He had added one. The molar mass of a compound was the sum of the molar masses of the atoms in its formula, and the formula had two oxygens in it. He wrote 12.01 plus two times 16.00, ran it through, and got 44.01 grams per mole. Then 132 divided by 44.01, which came out to three, exactly, cleanly, the kind of number a teacher puts in a problem on purpose.

He checked it a second time by rebuilding it from nothing. 12.01. Two times 16.00. Sum, 44.01. Three moles. It held. The wrong answer and the right one had both come out of him, out of the same head, and only one of them was true, and the difference between them was that in one of them he had actually looked at what he was counting. He could feel both habits sitting there, the rushing and the checking, and he could not honestly say the rushing was gone. It was more like the checking had learned to interpose itself, to step between his hand and the answer and ask a question first.

He texted Karma: three moles. The reply came back fast: "good. it's the oxygen doubling. everyone does it once." Everyone does it once. He read that twice, then folded the worksheet along its crease and slid it into his binder, with the loose leaf, with the molecule in the margin showing its two O's.

His grandfather folded the paper. "Sorted?" Cameron said he thought so, for this problem, and that Monday would tell him about the rest. His grandfather nodded slowly, took both mugs to the sink, and turned the tap on.

"Same time tomorrow," he said. "I'll make the good tea."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: London lies at about 51.5 degrees north, farther north than any point in the contiguous United States.
story:
The quarry had filled with spring rain again, and Mr. Popescu had declared it, for one afternoon only, an ocean. Hannah sat on the ledge with the current map spread across her knees, its paper rippling in the wind like something alive. "You're supposed to be practicing," Pierce said, dangling his sneakers over the green water. "Not staring at London like it owes you money."

"London does owe me money," Hannah said. "Two pounds. From a school trip. But that's not the point." She traced a finger along the red ribbon on the map, the warm current sliding up the Atlantic. "Mr. Popescu says I have to explain the whole Gulf Stream thing on Friday, and I can't even convince myself."

Eshan arrived with a bag of crisps and a laminated world map he'd stolen from the geography room, or borrowed, depending on who was asked. He would equivocate on the subject all afternoon, Hannah thought, saying "temporarily relocated" with such sincerity that even the ceiling tiles seemed to believe him. He flopped down beside her and pinned his map with a flat stone. "Show me the problem," he said, crumbs scattering. "Pretend I'm a very ignorant audience."

Hannah laid his map beside the current map and put one finger on London, one on the top of the United States. "Okay. Watch this. London sits at about fifty-one and a half degrees north." She slid her second finger up the American coastline, past Maine, past everything, until it crossed into Canada. "Farther north than any point in the contiguous United States. The whole lower forty-eight. All of it is south of London."

Pierce leaned over, frowning, and put his own finger on the map to check, as if Hannah might be cheating. "That can't be right. That's basically the US-Canada border."

"London is farther north than the border," Hannah said. "Than any spot in the contiguous states, all the way from Maine to the Pacific."

"That's deranged," Pierce said, with feeling. "London is fog and tea and rain. Canada is snow and moose. They can't be at the same latitude."

Eshan tossed a crisp into the quarry pool and watched a crow consider it. He was, as far as anyone could tell, thinking. Later, sitting on the bus home, Eshan would describe this moment to his sister as the moment Hannah's brain caught fire, though at the time he mostly noticed that she had gone quiet in a way that was slightly alarming.

From where Eshan sat, it looked like this: Hannah stared at the two maps, then stood up, holding the current map over her head like a banner. "That's the hook," she said. "That's how I start the presentation. I tell them where London is, they argue with me, and then I show them this warm river in the ocean and say, here, this is why the surprise exists. The warm water goes north." She paused. "I mean, I still have to explain the rest. The mechanics. Mr. Popescu will want the whole chain of reasoning, and I can't just gesture at a red squiggle and take a bow."

"That's literally what you just did," Pierce said. "You gestured at a red squiggle and took a bow."

"My bow was metaphorical." She sat back down and smoothed the map. "The thing is, I want to be careful. Everyone blames the Gulf Stream for everything, warm winters, cold summers, the price of cheese, and I don't want to overclaim. It's like apportionment. You have to divide up the causes honestly, give each thing its fair share, and admit where the ledger goes fuzzy." She tapped the paper. "Some of it I can say for sure. Some of it I'd just be making up, and I'd know it, and everyone claps anyway, which is worse."

Mr. Popescu came up the path then, carrying a thermos and looking delighted to find three teenagers voluntarily near a map, an event he would later compare to spotting a rare bird. "How goes the ocean?" he asked.

"It's a puddle," Pierce said. "It's a noxious green puddle with one crow and half a crisp in it."

"It's the Atlantic," Hannah said, "in spirit." She showed him the starting line she'd planned, the bit about London, and he raised his eyebrows and said nothing, which was how he expressed approval, or possibly the desire for tea. Hannah rolled up the map and slid it into a cardboard tube Eshan had thoughtfully brought for exactly this purpose, though he insisted, when asked, that it was originally for posters.

They walked back along the quarry rim as the light went long and orange, the water below turning from green to pewter. "So Friday," Eshan said, "when you're up there in front of everyone. What are you going to say when somebody asks the question you can't answer?"

Hannah swung the tube like a baton. "I'm going to say, that's the part where I stop guessing," she said. "And then I'll point at Pierce and say, but he still owes me two pounds, and everyone will forget what they asked."

"I owe you nothing," said Pierce, already running.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: The European Union's AI Act, which entered into force on August 1, 2024, bans some uses of AI outright, including social scoring of people.
story:
The clipboard went up beside the schedule on Monday, and Tyson read it twice before it meant anything. Numbers next to every name, his own included, ranked from Ayah at ninety-four down to Marisol at fifty-one. Below that, in Ms. Han's cramped hand: Productivity and Conduct Scores reflect camera and scanner analytics. Top scorers receive weekend shifts.

"Weekend shifts are the good ones," Tyson said.

"Congratulations," Ayah said. "You're thirty-eighth."

He was sixty-second, out of seventy-one. The weekend meant time-and-a-half on Sundays, and the Sunday money was what he had promised his mother he would bring in for the fall textbooks. He took a photo of the clipboard with his phone, on the theory that things you photograph become problems you can solve.

The cameras had arrived in March, small black domes that the installers had bolted above the registers without much ceremony. Tyson remembered his interview that winter, before any of it existed, Ms. Han across the desk in the tiny back office telling him he seemed like a kid who would show up. "That's most of it," she had said. "The rest I can teach." She had seemed, in her dour way, to be doing him a favor. Now she walked the aisles with a tablet that showed her, apparently, who was standing still.

The scoring made itself felt in small ways first. If he chatted with a customer for more than ninety seconds, his score ticked down. If the gap between scanned items widened, same thing. Ayah, who worked the register next to his, had developed a system of moving her hands constantly, wiping the belt, straightening the candy display, a performance of diligence aimed upward at the domes. "I call it interpretive retail," she said, and Tyson laughed so hard he lost two points for idle time.

That night he searched the store's vendor name and found a page on the software's own website describing a school district client that ranked students by their online behavior. A forum thread underneath it had gone sideways, one commenter insisting the whole category was banned somewhere. Tyson followed the link. The European Union's AI Act, the article said, had entered into force on August 1, 2024, and it banned some uses of AI outright, including social scoring of people. He read the sentence three times, then said it out loud to his empty room, testing it.

"It's called the AI Act," he told Ayah at break the next day, phone flat on the milk crate between them. "European Union. It entered into force on August 1, 2024. It bans some uses of AI outright, including social scoring of people. Like that clipboard."

"So we sue?"

"We don't sue. We're not in Europe."

Ayah looked at him with a patience that suggested she was the one being patient with him. "Then why did you learn it?"

He didn't have a good answer. He had assumed, somewhere in the middle of reading, that a rule this clear would travel, that if a thing was banned outright for being wrong in Brussels it would at least be embarrassing in New Jersey. But the article was about Europe, and the clipboard was here, and between the two stretched nothing but the vendor's confidence and Ms. Han's tablet. At the same time he couldn't pretend the ranking was meaningless. He had watched Marisol, the slowest scanner because she stopped to help old ladies find the prune juice, sink toward the bottom of the board, and he had watched a kid who never spoke to anyone climb, and the system was, in its dumb arithmetic way, teaching all of them what kind of person to be.

He went to the office anyway. Ms. Han looked up from the tablet, and he put his phone in front of her with the article open.

"I know," she said, before he said anything. "Corporate sent a memo. We're not covered by that law."

"So it's fine?"

"I didn't say fine." She set the tablet down. "I said covered."

Tyson stood there holding the distinction in both hands like something he had to carry home without dropping. He had wanted her to have either the sagacity to agree with him or the authority to shut him down, and she had offered neither, only that gap between legal and right, which was apparently his to walk around in.

"Do I get my Sundays back or not?" he asked.

"Score seventy and they're yours."

"Marisol helps people. That's why her score is low."

"That," Ms. Han said, "is above my pay grade," and picked the tablet back up.

He found Marisol at the register, showing a woman where the prune juice was, taking her time about it. The dome above them hummed, or seemed to. Tyson picked up a rag and started wiping the belt, next to Ayah, both hands moving.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
