fact: Blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals.
story:
Tristan's grandmother had offered the parlour of her house before he could even ask, clearing the china cabinet back against the wall so the living room could stand in for a stage. The community theatre's real space was booked until Thursday, and scene two could not wait until Thursday, because scene two was where his actors kept colliding. He had marked the boundaries of the playing area with masking tape on the rug, a rectangle of silver-grey that smelled faintly of lavender and old carpet, and he stood at the edge of it now with his script rolled in one fist.

"From the doorway, Delilah, you cross to the chair," he said. "Kasey, you rise when she's halfway there. Not before."

Kasey, who had been sprawled on the armchair like someone with no bones, sat up. "Why halfway? Last night you said when she reaches me."

"Last night she reached you and you stood up and you were in the same spot and you nearly knocked the lamp over." Tristan tapped the tape with his toe. "That's the whole problem. Nobody's in the wrong, exactly. Everyone's just somewhere no one planned."

Delilah, still in her coat because the parlour ran cold, frowned at the tape lines. "So what do we even call this? Is there a word for it, or are we making it up?"

"Blocking," Tristan said. "It's the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage. The director sets it during rehearsals." He felt a small private steadiness saying it, the way a word you learned only last week can already feel like a tool in your hand. Mr. Addo, who ran the theatre's young directors program, had written it on the whiteboard in a single line and then wiped it away, as if to say the rest was theirs to find.

The trouble was that Delilah, when she actually moved, did not move the way she had moved in his imagination. In his head she crossed the room like a struck match, quick and bright. In his grandmother's parlour she drifted, pausing at the window, trailing her fingers along the sill where the light came through in dusty bars, and by the time she reached the chair, Kasey had already been standing for ten awkward seconds, and the line that belonged to her sitting had to be delivered to the top of his head. Tristan called a halt and sat down on the piano bench to think.

He had read two books on directing, borrowed from Mr. Addo's office, and the books disagreed with each other in a way he found both maddening and oddly comforting. One said the director's plan was law, that spontaneity was a confounder to be eliminated before opening night. The other said plans were cages, that actors found truth only where the director had failed to predict them. Kasey, who had lurked over Tristan's shoulder during lunch, championed the second book with the fervour of the truly intransigent. "You're killing it," he'd said. "You're blocking the blocking, man." Delilah, meanwhile, defended the first book, which surprised him, since she was the one wandering to windows.

Tristan tried to forestall the argument by holding up both hands. "Different plan," he said. "Delilah, go to the window. That's not a mistake, that's the scene. You're drawn to the light, you're stalling, you don't want this conversation. Kasey, you stand when her hand leaves the sill. That's your cue. Not halfway, not when she reaches you. Watch her hand."

They ran it. Delilah crossed toward the chair, veered, stopped at the window, laid her palm flat on the sun-warmed sill, and something changed in her shoulders, a settling, as if the gesture had given her the character's reluctance for free. When her fingers lifted, Kasey rose, and for the first time all week the two of them occupied the stage like people who knew where the other one was. The lamp remained upright. The line landed in the right direction. Tristan, on the piano bench, felt the hair on his arms rise, that small animal recognition of a thing working.

"So my idea was right," Delilah said afterwards, pleased, still touching the windowsill.

"It wasn't right or wrong. You're a worse actor when I tell you exactly where to put yourself, and Kasey's better for it. That doesn't make a rule." Tristan looked at the tape rectangle on his grandmother's rug, at the scuffed silver lines crossing where the two paths had been redrawn. He suspected the truth was more crooked than either book admitted: that he would have to decide, scene by scene, which impulses to build on and which to shape, and that he would sometimes get it backwards, and that there was no way to know in advance which was which.

Then his grandmother came in with a tray of shortbread and stopped dead in the doorway, looking at the tape, at the moved china cabinet, at Delilah standing in the window light like a woman waiting for a train.

"We're doing a play," Tristan said.

"I can see that," she said, and set the tray down just outside the tape.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice.
story:
The line for the youth government forum stretched across the marble floor of city hall, past the plaque commemorating the building's hundredth year and under a chandelier that Eric kept glancing at, wondering how anyone changed its bulbs. He had signed up late, mostly because Angelina had insisted, and now he stood in a corridor that smelled of floor wax and old paper, holding a packet with his name misspelled on the label. Inside the packet was the topic he'd drawn by lottery: compare how a parliamentary system and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government. He had until the afternoon session to figure out what he actually thought.

"Trade you," Angelina said, leaning over his shoulder. Her topic was electoral reform, which she'd been arguing about since tenth grade, but Eric shook his head. She wanted an easy win for the debate showcase, the one the local paper sometimes photographed, and he understood that. Still, something about his topic snagged him, the way a loose thread does. Two systems, both calling themselves democracies, both producing a leader, and yet the machinery underneath was entirely different. He wanted to see the gears.

The morning workshop was held in a committee room with recalcitrant window blinds that refused to lower no matter how the facilitator tugged the cord. Mr. Leblanc, a city clerk who had volunteered to shepherd the students through the day, finally gave up on the blinds and simply moved the projector. He was a heavyset man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, and he refused to lecture. "You have the packet," he said. "You have each other. I'm here to resuscitate the coffee machine if it dies again."

Eric sat across from Audrey, a classmate he knew mostly from sharing a lab table in chemistry, and spread his notes between them. In a parliamentary system, he'd read, the legislature picked the prime minister, which meant the head of government could be swapped out by a vote of no confidence, sometimes in a single afternoon. He tested this aloud, sketching it on a napkin: "So the same body that chooses can also remove. The leader never really separates from the parliament." Audrey frowned at the napkin. "But isn't that dangerous? Fifty percent plus one and the whole government collapses?" It was a fair question, and Eric didn't have an answer, only a fascination with the fact that in some countries a government could fall between breakfast and dinner.

Then he turned to the presidential system and hit something that stopped him. In the American form, the president was elected separately from the legislature, fixed terms, and removal required impeachment, this long, deliberate process. But there was a footnote in the packet's reading list, a citation he almost skipped: the 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice. He read it twice himself.

He looked up. "Wait. So even if a president is enormously popular, that's it? Two elections and done?" Audrey shrugged. "Seems wasteful. If people want someone, why can't they keep choosing them?" Eric turned the amendment over in his mind the way he turned a proof in geometry, looking for the thing that didn't follow. What struck him was the difference in direction. A parliamentary system removed leaders quickly, from inside the legislature; a presidential system removed them slowly, through a formal process, and the term limit removed them automatically, regardless of popularity. One system trusted the parliament; the other, in a way, trusted the calendar.

"I don't know which I'd pick," he admitted. Audrey tapped the napkin. "Then say that. Say you don't know." It occurred to Eric that this might be the most honest thing he could say in the afternoon session, that both systems were answering the same fear, the fear of a leader who won't leave, but they answered it with different assumptions about people.

At the showcase, the committee room filled with students, parents, and two members of the actual city council who sat at the back looking professionally attentive. Angelina went first and was excellent, crisp and confident, and when she finished she shot Eric a thumbs-up from her seat, her want for the day already half satisfied. When Eric's turn came, he stood at the front with his napkin, smoothed flat, and explained the two machines. He described the prime minister who could fall in a day and the president who served a fixed term. Then Angelina raised her hand from the second row, playing devil's advocate as she'd promised to do for him.

"Why can't a popular president just keep running forever if the people want him?" she asked, loudly enough that a council member looked up from his phone.

"Because the 22nd Amendment, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice," Eric said. "Popularity doesn't come into it. It's a hard stop." He paused, expecting the room to react, and what he noticed instead was the small pleasure of watching people absorb it, Audrey nodding slowly, Mr. Leblanc at the doorway with his refilled coffee mug. Eric added his conclusion, or rather his non-conclusion: that the parliamentary way was faster, the presidential way more stable, and that he genuinely could not decide which mattered more, though he now understood that the choice revealed what you believed about how much power to trust to majorities and how much to time itself.

Afterward, Angelina found him by the water fountain, still glowing from her own round. "You should have picked the boring topic after all," she said, and grinned. "That was better than mine." Down the corridor, Mr. Leblanc was once more wrestling with the blinds, pulling the cord in short, stubborn jerks while the slats clattered and held their height, and Eric watched him think for a moment before walking over to hold the ladder.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Eye-contact norms differ: steady eye contact often signals confidence in North American interviews, while in some East Asian settings prolonged direct gaze at a senior person can seem impolite.
story:
Robert sat at the dinner table pushing rice around his plate while his father described the interview in terms usually reserved for surgery. Tuesday, three o'clock, the hardware store on Miller Road. Ten applicants for one position. You have to look the man in the eye, his father said, tapping the table twice for emphasis. Men who look at the floor look like men who steal.

His grandmother, visiting for the month, made a small sound of disagreement around her dumpling. She said, in Cantonese, that staring at an older person like that was rude, that when she was young you looked at the chin, or the knot of the person's tie, and answered clearly. His father laughed and said this was Canada, and she said she had noticed, and the two of them held their positions with the mutual affection of people who had argued about this for thirty years. Robert, whose chopsticks hovered between the two cuisines his mother had laid out, said nothing. He had an interview in two days and two sets of instructions that were exact opposites.

After dinner he called Hanna, who had worked at the library since she was sixteen and considered herself the household expert on getting hired. Look them in the eye the whole time, she said. Firm handshake. Say "I'm a fast learner" even if it's a lie, because it's a lie everyone expects. He wrote this down. Then, because he could not sleep, he texted Paisley, whose parents had moved from Seoul before she was born, and who answered at eleven with a paragraph about her uncle's interviews. She said her uncle used to look at the desk when the manager spoke and it wasn't nervousness, it was manners. Prolonged direct gaze at a senior person, in that setting, reads as challenge, she wrote. Then: but you're interviewing here, so honestly I don't know. That last part interested him more than the advice.

The question kept him awake in a way that felt almost pleasant, like a puzzle box. What was eye contact actually for? Was it a signal of honesty, the way his father believed, or a signal of deference, the way his grandmother had been taught? Both could not be true at once, and yet both of them were, somewhere. He wondered whether the manager on Tuesday would be the kind of man who read a steady gaze as confidence or as something cheeky, and he realized there was no way to know in advance, which struck him as an absurd gap in the whole system. You were supposed to present yourself to a stranger without knowing the grammar of the stranger's reading.

On Monday he practised with Ms. Sutherland, his old neighbour, who had agreed to play the manager over lemonade on her porch because his mother had asked and because she was, she admitted, bored. She asked him where he saw himself in five years, and he looked directly at her and delivered the answer Hanna had drilled, and she said it was very good and very hollow. She asked why he wanted the job. He looked at her again and said the true thing, that he needed money for textbooks and liked fixing things, and she set down her glass. That one, she said. That one has a floor under it.

He tried an experiment then. On the next question he kept his eyes on hers while she spoke, then dropped them when he answered, the way his grandmother did, chin or collar, never the floor. Ms. Sutherland tilted her head. It didn't read as shy, she said slowly. It read as careful. She asked where he had learned that, and he said his grandmother, and she said the strange thing was that it worked, and he felt something click open in his chest, not a solution exactly, but a door onto a room where the two sets of advice were not opposites at all. Look at the question. Look away from the answer. He wondered if he was inventing a style out of scraps, some affectation assembled from two inherited manners, and whether the manager would see a person or a collage.

Tuesday came fast. The store smelled of sawdust and fertilizer, and the manager was younger than Robert expected, maybe thirty, with a lanyard and tired eyes. When he asked the first question, Robert held his gaze, steady, the way his father had demonstrated over the salt shaker. When he answered, he let his eyes rest on the counter between them, then came back up at the end. He said "I'm a fast learner" once, early, and then abandoned the script and said that he had rebuilt his grandmother's radiator fan last summer with a manual and a borrowed socket set. The manager wrote something down.

Walking out, Robert did not know whether he had the job. The manager had not said, only that he would call by Friday, which augured nothing either way, and Robert caught himself already composing two versions of the story for the dinner table, one for his father and one for his grandmother, and then deciding he would tell it the same way to both and let them argue about what it meant.

At home he found his grandmother in the kitchen reheating tea. How did it go, she asked. He said he had looked at the man's eyes when he listened and away when he spoke, and she considered this for a long moment, stirring nothing. Like a compromise, she said. Like a person, he said, and she almost smiled. The phone was on the counter between them, silent.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Higher interest rates pay savers more, so households tend to shift some money from spending into savings, which lowers demand for goods and helps slow price rises.
story:
The flyer arrived taped to Natalie's pay stub: effective that Friday, the savings account rate at Meridian Trust would go up. She stood at the staff room counter with her apron of teller pins and read it twice, because the number she had memorized in June, when Mr. Lau hired her for the summer, had been smaller. Through the half-open door she could hear the lobby, the soft chime of the queue system, Dalton restocking deposit envelopes with his usual insouciant whistling, as if the folders of paperwork behind him belonged to somebody else.

Her phone was three years old. The charging port worked only when the cable was angled against the water bottle in her backpack, and the screen had a hairline crack running through the keyboard so that the letter e sometimes registered twice. She had been saving toward it since spring, slowly, the way you save when you are eighteen and earning teller wages. Now the flyer sat on the counter between her and the phone like a fork in a road she hadn't known she was standing at.

She mentioned it to Dalton on break, outside on the loading dock where the smokers went though neither of them smoked. "Did you see the rate change?" she said. He shrugged. "More money for free, I guess. Cool." Something about his shrug bothered her, the sense that he thought the bank was doing him a favor, and she found herself, without quite deciding to, defending the opposite view. "It's not free. Mr. Lau was in a meeting about it all Tuesday. The central bank raised rates and ours followed." Dalton ate his chips and waited, because he knew she wasn't finished.

Here was what she had been turning over, and she said it out loud for the first time. "When rates go up, savers get paid more. So people like me, with a paycheck, start moving some money out of spending and into savings. And if everyone's spending less on stuff, there's less demand for goods, and that helps slow down how fast prices rise. Inflation. That's the whole point." Saying it, she heard how it landed on her own case: her phone money could sit in savings now, earning more, or it could go out the door to the store on Saturday. The same policy that made saving sweeter was counting on her doing exactly that.

Reilly came in that afternoon to deposit her café tips and stayed to lean against the velvet rope, delighted, as always, to narrate Natalie's employment. "Tell her about my phone," Natalie said, and laid it out, the crack, the rate, the math she'd done on a deposit slip during a slow stretch. Reilly's position was simple: live now, buy the phone, you only have one youth. "That's not an argument," Natalie said. "That's a vibe." But she was honest enough to admit, watching Reilly's face, that some of her own irritation was envy. Reilly's insouciance, if that was the word, had a kind of cleanliness to it. Whereas Natalie had begun to notice that every dollar she spent now carried a small argument with her future self, and she wasn't sure when she had been sensitized to that, or whether it was wisdom or just another form of worrying.

The problem was that she couldn't tell which perspective was actually hers. Her mother texted that evening: "Rates are up, good time to be a saver, that's what my father always said." Her mother had never once, in Natalie's memory, followed her grandfather's advice. And Mr. Lau, when she asked him at closing whether the rate hike meant she should put her phone fund into savings, had only said, "That's your call, Natalie. I just work the hours." He was careful that way, allergic to telling anyone what to do with money, though she had watched him talk a widow through a bond ladder that morning with the patience of someone laying out stones.

She walked home the long way, past the phone store with its lit glass and its display model of exactly the phone she wanted, and she stood there for a minute letting herself want it, fully, without apology. Then she kept walking. At home she moved most of the checking balance into savings, but not all of it; she left enough for a good used phone from the shop Reilly's brother swore by, if one turned up. It felt less like a decision than like a truce between two people who both lived inside her, and she knew, going to sleep, that she couldn't prove the truce would hold. Maybe she'd drain the savings by August. Maybe she'd end up with a worse phone and more money and be glad, or be sorry. She couldn't know yet, and saying so to herself, out loud in the dark room, felt strangely like the first honest thing she'd done all week.

The next morning Dalton found her at the teller window and slid a folded deposit slip across the marble. "I did the math like you said," he told her. "Moved my concert fund into savings." He had written, in the margin where customers were supposed to sign, "for later," and underlined it twice.

"Oh yeah?" Natalie said, and reached for her stamp.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Simon Schama's Citizens, published in 1989 for the Revolution's bicentenary, argued that violence was an essential part of the Revolution from 1789 onward.
story:
Michael had spread eleven books across the library table like a general planning an invasion, and Mr. Morningstar, passing with a trolley of returns, paused to look at the carnage. "The French Revolution," he said, "in one essay. Ambitious." He slid one book out of the stack, tapped its cover, and put it back upside down, which Michael chose to interpret as a test of his attention.

The assignment said: explain how views of the Revolution had changed since 1800. Not what happened, but what people thought about what happened, which felt like standing in a hall of mirrors and being asked to describe the room. Michael had started with the simple version, the one from every documentary his father watched with his shoes off: the Revolution was good, then it went bad, the Terror was a detour, and Napoleon was the parking lot at the end of the detour. He had two pages of this and a sullen feeling that it was wrong, or worse, boring.

Angel arrived at three with a milkshake and no intention of studying, but she sat down anyway because the library was warm and Michael looked like a man losing a war. "What's the essay about?" "Historiography." "Gesundheit." He explained, and she sucked her straw with the gravitas of a supreme court judge. "So you're writing about writers arguing about killers arguing about a king." "Basically." "That's actually kind of great," she admitted, and stole one of his books, the fat one with the painting of a crowd on the cover.

Mathis texted from the museum where he was doing a volunteer shift, and his message sat on Michael's phone like a note passed in class. "you will not believe this. some guy at the guillotine exhibit is yelling at a tour guide. he says the terror was a DETOUR. other guy says no way. come get this its free entertainment." Michael showed Angel. She said, "We're going," already putting on her coat, and Michael, who had four books open, found himself carrying two of them in his backpack because leaving them felt like abandoning soldiers.

At the museum the argument had settled into a standoff between a man in a corduroy jacket and a woman with a lanyard, both arms crossed, the guillotine display between them like a referee. The man was saying the violence of 1793 was a betrayal of 1789, a corruption of the original promise. The woman said, "Read Schama. Citizens, published in 1989 for the bicentenary. He argued the violence was there from the start, essential to the Revolution from 1789 onward." The man said that was revisionist nonsense, and the woman said that was literally the point of the assignment her daughter was doing, and then she caught sight of Michael's backpack, from which the corner of a very fat book was emerging, and she pointed at it and laughed.

On the bus back, Angel read over Michael's shoulder as he typed into his phone, and she dictated corrections in the voice of a person who thought "the Revolution, per Marx" needed more commas. He was drafting a new thesis: maybe the argument between those two strangers was the whole essay. Some historians saw the Terror as a tragic wrong turn; Schama, at least, saw it as something the Revolution carried within it from the beginning. Both positions were about the same events. Both were, in their way, about the present in which they were written. Michael did not write that last part down. He suspected it but could not yet prove it, and he was tired of pretending certainty he did not have.

The librarian, stamping returns at the desk, had become Michael's unacknowledged ally over three afternoons, mostly by never shushing Angel, who deserved shushing. When Michael brought the fat book back, Mr. Morningstar weighed it in one hand. "Verdict?" "I think I agree with him," Michael said, "except when I don't, and I can't always tell which is which." "That's not a bad place for a sixteen-year-old," said Mr. Morningstar. "It's a terrible place for a certainty salesman." He stamped the book, and the sound was small and decisive, like a gavel in a very minor court.

The finished essay sat on the desk at home, and Michael read the last paragraph aloud to Angel on the phone, mostly to hear whether the sentences held their shape in the air. "So you don't know if you're right," she said. "I know that both stories are true to someone," Michael said, "and I know which one I lean toward, and I know I'd be lying if I pretended the leaning was proof." There was a pause, and then the sound of a straw hitting the bottom of an empty cup. "Put that in the essay," Angel said. "Word for word. Then go to sleep." He hung up, looked at the paragraph, and reached for his pen.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
The enrollment form had been open on her screen for twenty minutes, and Amy had filled in everything except the submit button. She was eighteen on Saturday, eleven days before the election cut-off, which meant her first vote would land exactly where her mother said it wouldn't matter and her civics teacher, Ms. Bekele, said it would. Between those two positions she had been living for a week, and the form sat there like a question she hadn't finished asking.

She texted Emilie instead of deciding. Are you enrolling?

Emilie called her within a minute, the way she always did, as if typing were beneath a crisis. "I'm stuck on the same screen," Emilie said. "My dad says don't bother, one vote in however many million. Ilias says the opposite. He sent me this thing about Australia, actually, hold on."

Amy put her on speaker and pulled up another tab. "What thing?"

"Okay, here. Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925. And if you don't vote without a valid reason, you can be fined." Emilie paused. "Fined. Actual money. For not voting."

"That can't be right." Amy searched it herself, expecting a debunking site, and found the same sentence repeated across government pages and news archives. Since 1925. A fine. She sat back. Somewhere in her head, two arguments she had been holding apart clicked against each other, the way magnets do when you finally turn one around. "So there, skipping is a choice you pay for. Here, skipping is free."

"Which means here it's a real choice," Emilie said slowly. "Like the freedom to be lazy about it."

"Or the freedom to refuse." Amy was thinking of Ms. Bekele now, who had once said in class that a ballot could be a protest or a promise, and who had refused to say which it should be. Amy had found that evasive at the time. Now it seemed closer to probity than evasion, an honesty about what a teacher had no business deciding for her. "I don't know which one I'm doing yet."

She heard Emilie's brother yelling something in the background, and then Ilias was on the line, because of course he had been listening. "It's not lazy, it's rational," he said. "Your one vote doesn't catalyze anything. It's a rounding error."

"Then why are you enrolling?" Amy asked.

"Because it costs me nothing and it annoys my dad," Ilias said, and Emilie laughed, and Amy laughed too, and it struck her that this was the actual argument, the one underneath all the grandiose speeches about democracy she'd been half-skimming all week: a small thing you do because it costs almost nothing and because someone you love would rather you didn't. That wasn't a principle you could defend in an essay. It was just true.

"Wait, you're enrolling?" Emilie said to him.

"Filled it in this morning. Took four minutes."

Amy looked at the form. Her name, her address, her eligibility date, all of it already sitting in the boxes, waiting to be made real. She thought about Australia, about a whole country where the state said you must, and about her own country, which said only you may, and she understood suddenly that the second was harder, not easier, that a freedom without a fine meant you had to supply your own reason. Hers wasn't fully formed. Part of it was Ilias annoying his father, part of it was Ms. Bekele's unfinished sentence, part of it was her mother, whom she would not be voting like. She was honest enough with herself to know that last part might change by the next election, or the one after, and that she would vote anyway, and that both of those things could be true at once.

"I'm doing it," she said, to no one in particular, and clicked submit.

The confirmation page loaded slowly, then all at once: her name, her electorate, a message thanking her for enrolling to vote.

"Did you do it?" Emilie asked.

"Done. You?"

A pause, the sound of keys. "Done," Emilie said. "Ilias, stop looking over my shoulder."

"I'm witnessing history," he said.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: For Mexico's Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2, families build home altars called ofrendas with orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are believed to guide souls home.
story:
Edouard stood in his aunt's kitchen with a crate of marigolds at his feet and his grandfather's photograph facedown on the table, because he could not decide which way was forward. The whole house smelled of cempasúchil, sharp and sweet at once, and his cousins were already out in the courtyard arguing about the height of the arch. November first was tomorrow. Everything had to be finished by tonight.

His mother had assigned him the flowers. "You're the one with the careful hands," she had said, which was a kind way of saying he was the one who had not offered to help until the last minute. He had spent most of October avoiding this. His grandfather had died in June, quickly, between a Tuesday phone call and a Thursday morning, and Edouard had written nothing at the funeral, said nothing at the burial, and then gone home and slept twelve hours like something torpid, a thing that could only process grief by shutting down entirely.

He opened his phone. There was a message from Maxim, sent an hour ago, and he read it again now to avoid picking up the photograph.

"You ghosted the group chat for two weeks. Julie and I covered your lab writeup, which by the way was due today and which I submitted at 11:58 like a coward. But that's not why I'm writing. My abuela used to say you can't abrogate a promise to the dead. You told me in August you'd be the one to put your grandfather on the ofrenda this year. Your words. It's the 31st. Whatever your family is doing, do that part. Then text me."

Edouard typed, deleted, typed again. "I don't know if I believe any of it," he wrote finally. "The marigolds guiding souls home. It's a nice story."

Maxim answered within a minute, which meant he had been watching his phone. "Nobody's asking you to pass a test on it. My mom doesn't fully believe it either and she's been buying flowers since dawn. Also for the record the scent thing is the point. Bright and strong, that's the whole design. Like a highway made of smell. Anyway the deadline is tonight, not your opinion."

Edouard put the phone face down next to the photograph, so the two objects were side by side, and went outside to carry the crate to the courtyard, where the family was building the altar against the back wall. Three tiers of wooden tables, sugar skulls still in their plastic, his grandmother's papel picado from thirty years ago creased but intact. His aunt was directing traffic with a wooden spoon. "Flowers here, here, and along the front edge," she said, "heavy on the front, that's where the scent meets the room. You know why they're orange, sobrino? The color and the smell, both loud on purpose. The belief is they guide the souls home. Two days, first and second of November. So we don't get to be lazy tonight."

He worked without answering, cutting stems, packing them tight along the table's edge until the orange ran the whole length like a spilled sunset. His younger cousin handed him the photo at last, and Edouard set it on the second tier between the pan de muerto and a small glass of his grandfather's terrible brandy. He had expected to feel something arrive, some door opening. What came instead was smaller and stranger: he noticed that the marigolds closest to the photograph already looked right there, as though they had grown for that spot.

"You're staring," his cousin said.

"I'm checking the arrangement," Edouard said, which was partly true.

Later, when the candles were lit and the family had gone inside to eat, Edouard sat on the courtyard step with his phone and started a reply to Maxim. He wrote about his literature class, about how Ms. Bekele had taught them metonymy in September, the way a crown stands for a king, the way a room full of orange flowers could stand for a man who had loved his garden. He wrote that he wasn't sure whether he believed the soul actually traveled, and he wasn't sure it mattered whether he was sure, because his hands had done the work either way. Building it had been a kind of belief, or the nearest thing to it he had access to. He kept that sentence, then cut it, then kept it again. Behind him the marigolds held their scent into the dark, and the photograph sat in its small appointed place, waiting for a date to turn over.

He hit send. Then he stood, went back to the altar, and straightened the glass of brandy so it caught the candlelight.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: A 2001 review titled 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good', led by Roy Baumeister, found that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size.
story:
Jordon had stopped riding home with her on Tuesdays, and Zoey knew exactly which sentence had done it. It had been six words, tucked after five compliments about her erg piece, something like "your catch is late, still." Everything before it had been true too, and she had meant every word, but when she'd waved at Jordon the next morning, Jordon had looked at the floor and taken the long way to second period.

She called Spencer on Sunday and pulled the phone onto the kitchen floor, cross-legged. Spencer was lying on his own kitchen floor, he said, because the wifi reached better there, and his debate prep was scattered around him like fallen leaves.

"Say the whole thing again," he said. "Exactly what you told her."

"I said her drive was powerful. Her ratio was the best on the team. Her breathing was steady. Her slide control was clean. Her recovery was smooth. Then I said her catch was late." Zoey pressed her thumbnail into the grout. "One thing out of six."

"One thing out of six," Spencer agreed. "But people don't count like that. In debate we build a case on logos, the actual reasoning, and judges still vote on how the round felt." He sat up. "My coach says a speech can be perfectly structured and still lose. Feeling isn't arithmetic."

"That's useless, Spencer."

"I know. That's why I'm on your kitchen floor." There was a pause, and she heard him shuffling paper. "Look up that guy. Baumeister. We used him in a round last month, the neg read a card from him."

She typed the name with her thumb. The article came up on her mother's old laptop, a review from 2001, and she read the first page twice with her chin on her knees. Then she read it aloud to Spencer over the crackling line: "Bad Is Stronger Than Good."

"That's the one," Spencer said.

The review said what the title said, and what her Tuesday had already proved: negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of the same size. Six good minutes of rowing and one late catch, and only the catch had survived the night. She hadn't been wrong to say it. She had just handed it to Jordon bare, like a stone with no wrapping, and let it sit in her palm all week.

On Monday, Ms. Greco from next door was out on her porch sorting through a box of her daughter's old college books, and Zoey stopped to help because stopping was easier than going home and rehearsing again. Ms. Greco offered her lemonade and a paperback on marketing that she said her daughter had used to monetize a baking blog, back when blogs could still be monetized without shame. Zoey took the lemonade, not the book, but she sat for a while, because Ms. Greco's porch was quiet and Ms. Greco asked no questions.

What she worked out on that porch was not a script. It was more like a rule she had to hold with two hands, and she wasn't sure of both of them yet. One hand said: the truth is not a favor you withhold; Jordon rowed every day with a late catch, and none of the five compliments would fix that. The other hand said: because bad lands harder, the way you hand it over is part of the truth too, not decoration around it. A criticism delivered carelessly wasn't the same criticism delivered well. It was a heavier one.

She texted Jordon that night: Can I come by. It wasn't a question, punctuation-wise, and Jordon's reply came twenty minutes later: whatever.

Jordon's garage had the erg in it, because Jordon's mother liked the house quiet. Zoey sat on an overturned milk crate and waited while Jordon rowed a warm-up, the chain rattling its long familiar sentence, and she made herself watch the catch before she spoke. Late by half a beat, consistently, on the left side.

"Your catch," Zoey said, when the chain went still. "It's late on the left, half a beat, every stroke. That's the whole problem. Not your power, not your ratio. Just that."

Jordon kept her hands on the handle. "You said all that other stuff last week and then this."

"I know. And the other stuff was true, but I dumped this on you last, alone, like it cancelled the rest. It doesn't. It's one thing, it's specific, and it's fixable, and I'll sit here every Tuesday if you want someone to count beats with you."

Jordon looked at her for a long moment, then at her own hands. "Half a beat?"

"Every stroke. I counted."

Jordon set the handle down, swung her legs off the slide, and reached for the strap to reset her feet. "Fine," she said. "But you're counting out loud."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: Google added 'search by image' in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web.
story:
Avery had claimed the table by the periodicals because it was the only one with an outlet, and because from there she could watch the automatic doors open and close like a slow argument the library kept having with the weather. She had meant to finish her college forms. Instead her grandmother had sent her a photo at 7:40 in the morning, a shoreline swallowed in black water, with the caption "This is happening RIGHT NOW in Lisbon. Pray." Three of her grandmother's friends had already forwarded it back to Avery with additions, one with a crying emoji shaped like a heart.

"Sixteen shares in an hour," Ria said, leaning over Avery's shoulder with the interest of someone watching a nature documentary. "Your grandmother is very fast for someone who types with one finger."

"That's not typing, that's hunting and pecking," Sullivan said. He set down his backpack and the cardboard sleeve of three muffins he had bought as a peace offering for having eaten both of theirs last time. "Is it real?"

That was the problem. Avery wanted it to be fake, cleanly and provably, so she could send a gentle correction and everyone could go back to forwarding videos of cats in tiny hats. But wanting a thing to be fake was not evidence, and she had spent enough of senior year learning the difference. She turned her phone face down on the table, which bought her thirty seconds of reprieve from the notification buzz, and pulled her laptop toward her.

The library's computer station was policed, in the loosest sense, by Ms. Weiss, who sat at a desk labeled ASK ME ANYTHING and appeared to mean it. Avery had once asked her where the bathroom was and received a small printed map. Now she approached the desk with the phone held out like a specimen.

"My grandmother sent this. It says it's Lisbon today. I don't know how to find out if that's true."

Ms. Weiss looked at the drowned shoreline, then at Avery, and something in her expression shifted from librarian to co-conspirator. "You know," she said, "you can search the picture itself. Google added search by image in 2011. You upload the photo, or paste its link, and it shows you where else it appears on the web." She spun the mouse toward Avery rather than touching it, which Avery understood as a policy: show, don't do. "Try it and tell me what you find. I'll be honest, I'm curious."

So it became a group project, as things did. Ria dragged a second chair over with a screech that earned them a look from a man reading military history. Sullivan ate a muffin. Avery right-clicked the image, chose search by image, and then, when the results loaded, went quiet in a way that made both of them lean in.

The photo was everywhere. It was real, in the sense that it existed, and it was old, in the sense that the earliest pages carrying it were from years ago, some in Portuguese, some in Spanish, attached to stories about a different storm, a different year, a different coastline entirely. One site, austere and almost ascetic in its plainness, just rows of dates and thumbnails, showed the picture surfacing again and again, each time claimed as current, each time somewhere new. The flood in the photo had happened. The flood in the caption had not, or at least not to that shore, not that day.

"So it's a lie," Ria said.

"It's a borrowed true thing," Avery said slowly, surprising herself with the phrase. "The water is real. The 'right now' is the lie." She scrolled further, and here it got harder, because one of the older pages was in Portuguese and she couldn't read Portuguese, and another looked like a blog that could itself have been recycling it, and at some point the trail went dim. She could prove it wasn't Lisbon today. She couldn't prove where or when it was first taken, not from here, and she noticed that she didn't want to equivocate about that part. It would be easier to write "totally fake" and let everyone's suspicion of the internet do the rest.

Sullivan, mouth full of muffin, offered the useful cruelty: "So what do you send her? 'Dear Grandma, the ocean is real but the calendar is lying'?"

Avery typed, deleted, typed again. She settled on the link to the search results and one sentence: "The photo is real but old, it's not Lisbon and it's not today. Love you. Ask before you share?" Then she sat with her thumb over send, watching the cursor blink, aware that Ria was watching her watch it.

"Send it," Ria said. "If she's mad, she'll be mad in one finger. It'll take her an hour."

Avery sent it, turned the phone face up, and pulled the college forms back toward her, though she read the same line about intended major three times. Behind the desk, Ms. Weiss called out, "Well? What was it?" and Avery held up the phone, the drowned shoreline glowing on the screen, older than the morning that claimed it.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: If people trust a central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases, and that expectation itself helps keep inflation down.
story:
The heat had lasted four days, and by Saturday morning the sidewalk outside Joshua's house had turned into a slow river of people walking toward the lake. He and Amy had dragged the folding table out at nine, and by ten they had sold eleven cups at a dollar each. Amy was recounting the coins in the shoebox when Helen arrived on her bike, one sandal strap flapping.

"We need to raise the price," Amy announced, before Helen had even dropped the kickstand. "Two dollars. Cups, sugar, all of it costs more than it did last month. My mom says everything is going up again this fall."

Helen locked the bike and leaned on the table's edge. "So because you think everything will cost more, you want to charge more now. That's the thing my brother keeps going on about. He says that's literally how inflation feeds itself." She popped the tab on a warm root beer she'd brought from her own fridge. "He works at the credit union now, so he thinks he's a genius."

Joshua had been quietly filling the pitcher, and he stopped with the spoon halfway stirred. He had spent half of June trying to understand a single paragraph in his economics textbook, the one about the central bank, and it had refused to stick until this exact moment, standing in the sun with a box of quarters and two friends arguing in front of him. "Wait," he said. "Say that part again. About expecting things to cost more."

Amy folded her arms. "I expect the price of sugar to go up, so I raise my price, so you expect lemonade to cost more, so you charge more for whatever you sell. It goes around in a circle and everyone's prices climb like a ladder." She said it the way she said most things, as though the world had personally annoyed her.

"And here's the other half," Helen said, jabbing her root beer at him. "My brother says if people trust the central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller raises and smaller price increases, and that belief itself actually helps keep inflation down. It's not just the bank doing stuff. It's everyone believing the bank will do it." She shrugged. "I thought that was absurd when he told me. Believing something makes it true? But he made me read a whole thing about it."

Joshua set the spoon down and cogitated, visibly enough that Amy snorted at him. He was trying to hold both ideas at once: Amy's ladder, where expectation pushed prices up, and Helen's version, where trust in the bank pulled them down. The same force, running in opposite directions depending on what people believed would happen. "So the question isn't really what the bank does," he said slowly. "It's what we think the bank will do. That's the actual lever."

"That's what I said," Helen said, with the dignity of a person who had said something considerably less clear.

"Fine, that's what you said better than you said it." Joshua pulled the marker from under the table and turned the cardboard sign face down. "Okay, here's my problem. The parade starts at noon. Half the town walks past here in the next ninety minutes, and after that it's over, we're packing up. If we're going to change the price, it has to be now."

Amy pointed at the sign. "Two dollars. Costs are going up. I'm not running a charity."

Helen pointed at the same sign. "One dollar. If we hold our price, we're the one thing on this street that didn't get more expensive. People notice that. They trust us. They might even come back tomorrow, or tell their friends. We're the central bank of lemonade." She paused. "The lemon bank. The bank of lemon."

"You cannot call it that."

"The Bank of Lemon," Helen said, with great firmness, "is the cornerstone of this neighborhood's monetary system."

Joshua laughed so hard he nearly knocked over the pitcher, and then he stood there in the sun, marker uncapped, genuinely stuck. If he held the price, he was betting that being the steady thing would pay off in trust, in repeat customers, in some slow good will he couldn't count. If he raised it, he'd have more cash in the box by one o'clock, and he could see it, touch it, divide it three ways. The certain dollar versus the uncertain one. He thought about the paragraph in the textbook, which had finally stopped being a paragraph and turned into a shoebox full of quarters.

"I'll tell you what I actually believe," he said. "Holding at a dollar only works if people believe we'll hold at a dollar. The moment they think we're going to jump to two, they stop trusting us, and then honestly we might as well jump to two, because the trust is already gone. So whatever we pick, we pick it now and we stick to it all day. No changing it at eleven forty-five when the crowd shows up." He looked at them both. "That part I'm sure about. Which price, I'm honestly not."

Amy chewed her lip. Helen made him write, on the back of the sign, in his best handwriting, a solemn declaration that the price of one cup of lemonade would remain one dollar for the entire day, signed by all three of them, witnessed by a passing jogger who agreed to initial it and then asked if it was some kind of affidavit. Joshua said it basically was. The jogger bought a cup.

At eleven fifty the street filled, sun hats and strollers and a man carrying a tuba case, and the three of them poured in a steady rhythm, quarters ringing into the shoebox, ice melting fast, Amy calling out the price like a town crier. Somewhere past thirty cups Joshua did the math in his head, two dollars times thirty, and felt the small ache of the money they hadn't taken. He decided he'd figure out later whether it was a loss. A woman with a sunburned toddler came back for a second cup and said, "You're still a dollar? God bless you people."

Helen leaned over and whispered, "The Bank of Lemon thanks you for your trust."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The number of moles in a sample equals its mass in grams divided by its molar mass in grams per mole.
story:
The kitchen at her grandmother's house still smelled of the morning's coffee, and the afternoon light came through the lace curtain in a way that burnished the counter tiles to the color of honey. Taylor sat at the table with her chemistry worksheet flattened in front of her, a bag of flour, and her grandmother's old kitchen scale, the brass kind with sliding weights. She had come for the weekend to help clear the attic, but the worksheet had come with her, folded twice in her backpack, and it had refused to stay folded.

The problem wanted her to find how many moles of a product would form from a given mass of reactant. She had copied the method off the board on Friday, but by Saturday morning the notes looked like something written by a stranger. Ms. Sokolov had said something about it in class, something quick, and Taylor had written it down without hearing it, which was its own small failure.

"How much flour do you need," her grandmother asked, setting a bowl down beside the scale. She was making the bread she made every Saturday, and she had not asked why Taylor wanted the flour weighed first.

"Three hundred grams," Taylor said, because that was a number she could picture. She slid the small brass weight along the arm and watched it dip and hover, and added flour from the bag until the beam leveled. The scale held steady. Three hundred grams of flour, sitting there in the pan, exactly what the recipe wanted.

She looked at the worksheet again. The reactant in the problem had a mass, twenty-four grams, and a molar mass, forty grams in every mole. Her grandmother measured what she needed by mass because you could not count grains of flour; they were too small and too many. Taylor turned her pencil over and wrote the mass in grams above the molar mass, drew the line between them, and sat very still. If a mole was just the chemist's way of counting something too small to count, then the number of moles in a sample equals its mass in grams divided by its molar mass. That was the whole thing. Twenty-four divided by forty. She worked it out and wrote the answer, and the sliding weights on the scale seemed suddenly to have been waiting for her to notice them.

"So moles aren't animals," her grandmother said, reading over her shoulder without shame.

"Not in chemistry," Taylor said. "In chemistry they're an amount. That's the word. An amount of a substance."

Her grandmother laughed and punched down the dough. Taylor texted Kate a photo of the scale with the brass weights, and Kate texted back a row of exclamation points, and then, from the other room, Gemma called, because the three of them had a study call planned and Gemma had never once in her life been late for anything. Taylor put the phone on the windowsill and propped the worksheet against the sugar tin where both girls could see it through the camera.

Gemma had done the problem a different way, some proportion she had built from the back of the book, and for ten minutes they argued, not angrily, the way you argue when you both might be right. Gemma's proportion gave the same answer in the end, which annoyed Taylor more than if it hadn't, because it meant the method Ms. Sokolov had taught was not the only door into the room. Kate said very little, which meant she was lost, and Taylor found that explaining it out loud, with the flour still dusted on her knuckles, made it clearer in her own head than any rereading had. She could show it with her hands. Mass, divided by how heavy one mole is. She could point at the scale. But when Gemma asked why you were allowed to just divide, why it worked like that, Taylor said she didn't know yet, only that it did, and that she would ask on Monday.

The bread went into the oven and the attic waited, and Taylor sat listening to Gemma move on to the next problem, which was harder, and to her grandmother humming in the kitchen. In school the work had felt like metaphysics to her, things true in a world she couldn't visit, and here it was sitting in a brass pan on the counter, three hundred grams of it, level with the beam. She did not entirely understand what a mole was underneath, what made it the size it was, and she let that not-knowing sit beside her without trying to burnish it into certainty. The oven ticked. Somewhere upstairs, in the interminable afternoon of boxes and old coats, the attic went on waiting, and Taylor picked up her pencil and copied the next problem down.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed makes the distance needed to brake about four times as long.
story:
The parking lot behind the driving school smelled of hot asphalt and someone's microwaved lunch, and Eve sat in the driver's seat of a white Corolla with her hands at ten and two because that was the only thing about driving she was certain of. Ms. Bondarenko folded herself into the passenger side, set a clipboard on her knee, and said they would begin with braking. Not steering, not mirrors. Braking.

"Before you touch anything," Ms. Bondarenko said, "answer me this. If you double your speed, how much longer does the car need to stop? Guess. Everyone guesses wrong."

Eve thought of Riya, who had failed the written test twice and blamed the questions, and of Chantal, who had passed on the first try and now drove to school with one hand on the wheel like she was conducting an orchestra. Eve wanted to be Chantal. She also wanted, in a quieter way she didn't usually admit to, to be right for its own sake, the way she was right in physics class when everyone else guessed.

"Twice as long," she said. "Maybe a bit more."

Ms. Bondarenko smiled without warmth. "Everyone says that. It's about four times as long. Double the speed, quadruple the braking distance." She let the silence sit. "Now you know something most drivers on the road do not."

Eve's face went hot. She had wanted the answer to be simple, arithmetic, fair, and instead it was exponential, a fact that punished speed the way her mother's moods punished small confessions. She pressed the brake with her foot, gently, and felt the car dip its nose.

They drove out through the subdivision, past houses with friable brick walls shedding orange dust onto the sidewalks, past a dog tied to a stake that watched them with total indifference. Ms. Bondarenko made her stop at every unmarked corner, full stops, and Eve began to understand that the lesson wasn't about her feet. It was about imagining the future, about how far ahead of yourself the world already existed, invisible, arriving.

At a straight stretch of empty road, Ms. Bondarenko told her to accelerate to thirty, then brake hard at an orange cone. Eve did it. The stop came fast, the seatbelt biting her collarbone. "Again at sixty," Ms. Bondarenko said, and set a second cone four times farther out. Eve looked at the distance and something in her chest recalibrated. She accelerated, and the road became a different object than it had been at thirty, longer, faster, less obedient. When she braked, the car kept going, tires shuddering, and stopped well past where the first cone would have been, only just short of the far one. Her hands were shaking on the wheel.

"You see," Ms. Bondarenko said. "Same car. Same driver. Only the number changed."

They drove back mostly in silence, and Eve found herself thinking about the zeitgeist of her whole graduating class, the way everyone talked about leaving, about accelerating into their lives, gap years and cities and internships, as though speed were only ever gain. Chantal had eviscerated her at lunch last week for saying she might stay close to home for her first year. "You're already braking," Chantal had said, meaning it as a joke. Eve hadn't laughed. Now she wondered whether Chantal had any idea what braking actually cost, or whether she, Eve, had any idea what going fast did, and she suspected the honest answer was that neither of them did, that the two truths could sit in the same person without one canceling the other.

Back in the lot, Ms. Bondarenko signed the clipboard and said she was a natural at the wheel, which Eve recognized as a thing instructors said, and which she accepted anyway, because it was partly true. She had stopped where the cone demanded. She had not panicked. But pulling her bag from the back seat, she kept seeing the far cone sliding toward her past the windshield, the car refusing her foot, the world requiring four times what she had assumed.

She texted Riya from the curb: "failed nothing, learned I know nothing, same time next week." Riya sent back three crying-laughing faces. Eve put the phone in her pocket and stood a moment in the heat, watching a car turn into the lot, fast, much too fast for a school full of beginners.

"Some people never learn it," Ms. Bondarenko said, not looking up from her clipboard. "You learned it in one lesson. That's not nothing."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Raising interest rates tends to strengthen a country's currency by attracting foreign savings, which makes imports cheaper and puts downward pressure on prices.
story:
The automatic doors of Marché Brunelle exhaled warm air at Levi every afternoon at four, and by his second week of bagging groceries he had stopped noticing. He noticed other things instead: the way the price tags were changed on Tuesdays, usually upward, and the small red stickers on the imported olive oil that meant the store had ordered too much of something now too expensive to move. His father had been laid off in the spring, and Levi had taken the job without being asked, which was its own kind of conversation in their house, most of theirs being conducted that way, through silences and spartan gestures rather than sentences.

It was Ms. Pierre who complicated the job. She taught economics at his school and had announced in September that the grade eleven class would each give a five-minute explanation of a policy question, graded on clarity, not opinion. Levi had drawn the central bank. "You'll explain how raising interest rates slows inflation," she'd said, and he'd nodded as though this were a small thing, the way he nodded at the cash register when a customer asked for paper instead of plastic.

The problem was that he did not understand it. He understood the first half, the half every YouTube video repeated: rates go up, borrowing costs more, people spend less, prices stop climbing. It was rationalism itself, tidy and pleasing, cause and effect in a straight line. But the videos all stopped there, and something in him refused to stop with them. On Saturday he stood in aisle four holding a bottle of Greek olive oil whose price had dropped twice since August, and he could not make the tidy half of the theory account for it.

"Move your cart," said Marylou, who had appeared beside him with a basket containing, as far as he could tell, only marshmallows and a lemon. She worked the next register over. "You've been staring at oil for ten minutes. Customers think you're deeply religious about it."

"The price went down," Levi said. "Imported stuff. This is three dollars less than it was in the summer, and the chocolate's the same, and the coffee came down last week. Explain that to me while the whole country is having a meltdown about prices."

Marylou looked at the shelf with the polite attention she gave to things she intended to forget. "Maybe the store messed up."

"Twice? On three different imports?" He put the bottle in her basket without asking, which she allowed. "The central bank raised rates in the spring. Everybody at school was complaining because the loonie thing, the exchange thing, it changed after." He stopped, because a shape was assembling itself at the edge of his mind, incomplete but insistent.

He took out his phone in the stockroom during his break, away from Ms. Pierre's hypothetical frown, and looked up the Canadian dollar against the euro. It had strengthened. He read the line twice. Then a second line, from some financial site, gave him the rest in one flat sentence: higher rates had attracted foreign savings, and the stronger currency made imports cheaper. He sat on a crate of paper towels and let it turn over in him. Foreign money flowing in to earn the higher interest, a stronger dollar, cheaper olive oil, cheaper chocolate, prices pressed downward from the outside. The videos' tidy half was not wrong. It was just not the whole body.

On Sunday, Oceanne came in with her mother to shop for the school trip Ms. Pierre was organizing to France in the spring, forty students and a budget that had to be locked in by November. Oceanne found Levi restocking soup and reported, with theatrical despair, that the trip might actually be affordable now, because the exchange rate had improved after the rate hikes and their euros would go further. "Which makes no sense," she said, "because everyone says the economy is terrible."

"It does make sense," Levi said. "It's the same thing as the olive oil."

"The olive oil."

"Strong currency. Imports get cheaper. When you're in France, you're the one importing." He heard how clumsy it sounded, and how the clumsiness mattered. Ms. Pierre graded on clarity, and clarity was not the same as knowing. He could feel the two halves of the mechanism sitting side by side in his head, unwilling to merge into speech.

He practiced on Monday, at the register, in the gaps between customers. He explained it to the bread aisle, to the freezer cases, to Marylou, who said, "You said the same thing four ways, which means you don't know which way is the true one yet." He explained it to Oceanne over lunch, and she said, "Better, but you still sound like you're reciting a hostage statement." That evening he explained it to his father, who listened while fixing the kitchen tap, and when Levi finished, his father said only, "So the interest rate goes up, money comes in from other countries, our dollar gets stronger, and everything we buy from outside gets cheaper. And that pushes prices down." It was the first full sentence his father had produced about economics in Levi's lifetime, and it hung in the air between them, ordinary and enormous.

On the day of the presentation, Levi stood at the front of Ms. Pierre's classroom with the olive oil bottle he'd bought with his employee discount, and he set it on the desk like evidence. He gave the borrowing half first, because it was true and because his classmates needed the ground floor. Then he gave the second half, slowly, watching faces change. Rates rise, foreign savings flow in, the currency strengthens, imports get cheaper, and the cheaper imports press prices down. He told them about the aisle where he worked, about the red stickers, about Oceanne's trip, because the abstraction seemed to want a body, and the body was a grocery store. When Ms. Pierre asked afterward whether the second channel was larger or smaller than the first, he said he didn't know, and that he thought nobody entirely did, and she wrote something in her book without telling him what.

He walked home through the cold with the olive oil in his bag, past the bank with its window of exchange rates, and stopped for a moment in front of the glass. The numbers meant something to him now, though he was honest enough with himself to admit they did not mean everything. In his pocket, his phone buzzed with a message from Oceanne: a photograph of a baguette, taken in her kitchen, with the caption "practicing imports." He stood a second longer, then pulled his collar up and went on toward home, the bottle swinging gently against his hip.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing, in which new drivers move from a learner's permit to a provisional license with restrictions before a full license.
story:
The parking lot behind Hamlisch Driving Academy still held the morning's frost when Eli slid into the passenger seat of the white Corolla, permit folded into quarters in his jacket pocket. He had passed the written test two days earlier, after a month of practice questions at the kitchen table while his mother dried dishes behind him, and he had already promised things he had no right to promise. Nellie wanted a ride to the lake on Saturday. Kiptyn had claimed shotgun for the whole month of August, out loud, in the cafeteria, as though calling it made it binding.

"Seatbelt," said Mr. Tremblay, settling a clipboard on his knee. He was a wide man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead and a way of pausing before he spoke, as if filing each word in advance. "Mirror, seat, hands at nine and three. Then we'll do a loop around the block."

Eli adjusted the mirror and found his hands already at ten and two, the way his uncle had taught him on a farm road when he was twelve. Mr. Tremblay reached over without comment and moved his right hand down two inches. The engine started. Eli's foot hovered over the brake longer than it needed to, and then they were moving, the car gliding out of the lot with a smoothness that surprised him, as though the car had been waiting to be useful all night.

"You did your homework," Mr. Tremblay said at the first stop sign, when Eli came to a full and slightly theatrical stop. "Most first-timers roll it. You're tense, but you're precise." Eli took this as the compliment it probably was. At the second intersection he turned too wide and mounted the curb with a crack that went through his teeth, and Mr. Tremblay said nothing at all, which was worse than being lambasted, and Eli understood that now. He would have preferred to be yelled at. Yelling he could push against.

"Again," Mr. Tremblay said. They circled the block. On the third pass, the turn came clean, tires kissing the curb within a foot, and Eli felt something loosen in his shoulders. "Better. Tomorrow we take the hill on Garfield."

"There's no more today?" It came out more urgently than he meant.

Mr. Tremblay looked at him over the rims of his glasses. "You want to get somewhere, I think."

"My friends think I'm driving this weekend." Eli kept his eyes on the road ahead, on a duplex with a basketball hoop nailed above its garage. "Nellie and Kiptyn. I told them Saturday."

"You told them wrong." Mr. Tremblay's voice stayed level, almost gentle. "What you have is a learner's permit. You drive with a licensed adult beside you, like me, like your mother. That's it. After the road test you get a provisional license. Restrictions still apply, and they include passengers your own age. The full license comes after that, once the provisional period is done."

The silence in the car had a texture to it. Eli let the car drift forward a few feet before he remembered the brake. "Nobody said that at the DMV."

"Nobody ever reads the pamphlet." Mr. Tremblay tapped the clipboard. "It's called graduated licensing. Stages. You climb them."

Eli thought of the cafeteria, of Kiptyn's scathing reaction to any plan that fell through, the theatrical groan, the folded arms, the way disappointment in him always arrived dressed as contempt. And Nellie, who would say it was fine and then go quiet in a way that lasted days. He had been building the summer out of something he didn't actually have. He turned the corner again, tighter this time, and the car responded like it agreed with him.

"Can I tell them I'll have it by the lake trip in July?"

"That depends on your test date and your birthday and how you drive between now and then." Mr. Tremblay made a note on the clipboard. "You have perspicacity, kid. Most students, I tell them about the stages and they sulk. You're already calculating." He said it without warmth, which somehow made it more credible. "The calculating is the good part. The assuming you did before, that part you fix."

They pulled back into the lot. Eli sat with his hands still on the wheel while the engine ticked down, working out exactly what he would say to Nellie, then a second version for Kiptyn, then a third, simpler one, that just said the truth and let them decide what to do with it. He couldn't tell yet which version was honest and which was just smooth, and he suspected he wouldn't know until he heard himself say it out loud.

He took out his phone in the parking lot, thumbs over the screen, and typed, "About Saturday." Behind him, Mr. Tremblay locked the Corolla and called out, "Same time tomorrow. Hill on Garfield." Eli hit send.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on.
story:
The recipe box smelled of cardamom and pencil shavings, and Lily had carried it to the kitchen table before she fully decided to. Her grandmother had been dead eleven days. The apartment still hadn't acclimated to the absence; the chairs stood where the chairs had always stood, and the silence where her grandmother's radio used to hum seemed louder than sound. Lily slid the rubber band off the box and thumbed through the cards, each one in that looping, forward-leaning hand. Cardamom buns. Fish soup with dill. Pancakes thin enough to read a newspaper through.

"You're going to cook something," her mother said from the doorway. It wasn't quite a question. She had a garbage bag in one hand, the beginning of the great sorting, and she looked at the recipe box the way you look at a door you're not sure you want to open.

"I might," Lily said.

Her mother set the bag down, then picked it up again, then left the kitchen without saying either yes or no. That was the whole conversation, and Lily understood it anyway. Her mother wanted the apartment emptied before it could argue with her. Lily wanted, though she couldn't have named it yet, the opposite.

She texted Jovan a photo of the cardamom bun card. His reply came fast: are those her measurements?? "butter, enough." He added a row of laughing faces and then, separately, "for real though, are you okay? Kylan said you weren't at practice." She typed "I'm fine," deleted it, and typed instead, "Can you come over? I want to try making these and I don't want to do it alone."

Jovan arrived the next afternoon with Kylan and a paper sack of yeast he'd had to ask a cashier to help him find, since neither of them knew what yeast looked like outside of bread. Kylan, who considered himself a realist, leaned against the counter watching Lily fail at scalding milk. "Isn't it kind of morbid," he said, not cruelly, the way he said most things, "cooking a dead person's recipes?"

"It's not morbid," Lily said. "It's just a recipe."

"It's talking to her, though. You said you were going to talk to her while you did it."

"Fine, then it's talking to her." The milk had skinned over. She peeled the skin off with a fork, the way her grandmother had once shown her, without thinking, and the not-thinking was the part that undid her for a second. She held still until the second passed. "You think that's weird. You think grief is supposed to, like, taper off. Get smaller every month until it's gone."

"Isn't that the point? Moving on?"

"I don't know," Lily said, and found she meant it as an actual question, not a concession. "I've been trying to figure out what moving on even means. Like, if you forget the person, that's one thing. But if you keep them, in some small way, on purpose, is that failing to move on, or is it just a different way of doing it?"

Kylan shrugged and punched down the dough, which had risen beautifully, an event he took visible credit for. Jovan, meanwhile, had gone quiet over the recipe card, tracing the margin where someone, decades ago, had penciled "reduce salt for Müller" beside the fish soup.

"Mr. Müller," Lily said, catching it. "He used to trade them fish. She told me once. He'd bring mackerel from the market and she'd send soup back over the fence."

Mr. Müller still lived next door, and when the buns came out of the oven, browned and cardamom-scented and slightly lopsided, Lily carried four of them over on a plate and knocked. He took a long time answering. When he saw the plate his face did something complicated, softening and tightening at once, and he said, "Those are hers." Then, "Come in, come in, before they cool."

His kitchen was dim and very clean. He ate one bun slowly, and told her about the mackerel, and about her grandmother beating him at cards with a ruthlessness he described as virulent, smiling the whole time. "You have her hands," he said, nodding at the plate. "For the dough, I mean. Some people have the hands for it."

That night, after Jovan and Kylan left with buns in their jacket pockets, Lily sat at her laptop with flour still under her nails and typed, almost idly, "is it normal to talk to someone who died." She expected the internet's usual nihilism, some cold evolutionary account of grief as a malfunction to be corrected. What she found instead stopped her. A book from 1996, Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, which had argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on. She read the sentence three times. Not a failure. Normal.

She texted Jovan: "Continuing Bonds. It's a book. Look it up." Then she took the fish soup card out of the box and propped it against the sugar jar, where she could see it from the stove, and started a grocery list in her own handwriting beneath her grandmother's. Reduce salt for Müller, she wrote. The kitchen still smelled of cardamom, and she said, quietly, "Okay, so tomorrow we do the soup."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Concussion guidelines say an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine.
story:
The park rink had been flooded that morning and the ice already showed skate scars, gray threads stitched across the white, by the time Mya laced up for the playoff game. Her stick was her grandmother's, a wooden thing everyone on the team called anachronistic, though Mya had come to like the weight of it, the way it made her slow down and think before she committed to a pass. Mr. Reyes, who coached the winter league and taught chemistry at the high school, blew his whistle from the bench and pointed at the center circle. Mya skated out for the opening faceoff with the tournament bracket folded in her mind: lose today and the season ended before dark.

They were up by one at the end of the second period when Scarlet went into the boards. Mya saw it happen from the point, the way Scarlet's feet tangled with the opposing winger's, the way her helmet struck the plastic edging with a sound like a dropped melon. The whistle came fast. Scarlet got up on her own, which Mya would think about later, how getting up looked like being fine.

"I'm good," Scarlet said on the bench, pulling her glove back on before she'd even sat all the way down. "Put me in for the third. Coach, seriously. It's the last period."
