Mr. Reyes crouched in front of her and shone the little penlight from the first aid kit across her eyes. Scarlet tracked it, answered his questions about the score and the period and her own birthday, and kept saying she was fine, fine, put me in. There were eight minutes on the clock until the third started. Mya stood close enough to hear all of it, close enough to see that Scarlet's hands were shaking inside her gloves.

Mya remembered, then, the night in October when she'd stayed late to help Mr. Reyes clean out the equipment shed and found the league safety binder wedged behind a stack of pylons. She'd read it mostly out of boredom, standing under the one bare bulb, and one line had stuck because it was so flat and so final. She hadn't known it before. Nobody had ever told her, not in three seasons of playing.

"Scarlet," she said, and her voice came out lower than she intended. "Guidelines say you don't go back in the same day with a suspected concussion. Even if you feel fine. Same day, that's the whole point."

"That's for people who are actually hurt," Scarlet said. "I'm not hurt. I got up."

"That's not what the rule says." Mya had the strange sensation of arguing from a document she had read exactly once, in a shed, months ago. She could not remember the page number or the exact wording around the line, only the line itself, and she was honest with herself about that gap even as she kept talking. "It doesn't say only if you're dizzy. It says suspected. You hit your head."

Scarlet looked at the ice, then at the clock, then at her own skates. Mya watched her change, not all at once but in stages, the way the plastic they'd studied in chemistry went from separate monomers to something joined, each small unit clicking into the next until it held a shape. First Scarlet stopped pulling her glove on. Then she sat back. Then she said, very quietly, "If we lose this I'm going to be so mad at you."

"We might lose," Mya said. "We might not."

They didn't, as it happened. Mattea moved back to wing and scored into an empty net with forty seconds left, and the bench emptied onto the ice, and Mya stood at the blue line while everyone else piled into the corner. Mr. Reyes had tried to codify the no-same-day rule into the team's written plan that fall, she remembered, and the league had sent it back with notes, wanting the wording softer, wanting to leave room for coaches' judgment. She had thought nothing of it at the time. Now she wondered who had argued for the softer wording, and whether they had ever stood on a bench watching a sixteen-year-old pull her glove back on with shaking hands.

Scarlet skated over to her before the handshake line, still in her helmet because Mr. Reyes wouldn't let her take it off yet, just in case, he said, though he didn't say in case of what. "My mom's going to make me go to a clinic tomorrow," Scarlet said. "I have to sit in the waiting room while you're all at the semi-final."

"That sounds terrible," Mya said.

"It does." Scarlet bumped her shoulder against Mya's, a small collision, nothing like the boards. "Text me the score anyway."

"Every period," Mya said, and got in line behind Mattea.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Opportunity cost counts only the single next-best alternative given up, not all the alternatives added together.
story:
Claire sat cross-legged on her bed with the phone on speaker and her math homework shoved face-down beside her, because the numbers on the page were not the numbers that mattered tonight. "So you can only take one," Mahi said from the doorway, holding two mugs of tea she had clearly made to justify being nosy. "One. Saturday morning at the café, Saturday night at the bookstore, or Sunday at Mr. Pham's nursery. He asked me himself. Ten dollars an hour, all three of them." Claire pulled her pillow into her lap and hugged it. "The café shift is seven hours. The bookstore is five. Mr. Pham said six. So if I take the café, I'm missing five plus six, eleven hours, a hundred and ten dollars gone."

Mahi sat down on the end of the bed and handed her a mug. "That's a weird way to count." "It's the right way," Claire said, though she heard how quickly she said it, like a door pushed shut. "Every choice costs you everything you didn't pick. That's what it feels like, anyway." She wrote it out in her notebook, under a chemistry formula she had abandoned: café 70, minus 50, minus 60, equals minus 40. As if choosing her best option still left her in debt to the other two. The numbers sat there looking accusing, and she stared at them while her tea went lukewarm.

Then Kacey's name lit up the phone screen, and Claire answered on the first ring. "Tell me you're taking Sunday," Kacey said. "I'm working Sunday at the nursery too, he hired three of us, it's going to be so fun. And the bookstore wants you Saturday night? That's the poetry reading. Marcus is reading. You'd be paid to stand there and listen." "I know," Claire said. "That's the problem. I keep adding up everything I'm giving up and it's like a hundred and ten dollars plus a poetry reading plus you, and it makes every option look like a loss." There was a pause on the line, the kind where you can hear someone thinking. "Wait," Kacey said. "My brother did this exact thing in econ. You don't add them all. You only count the one next-best thing. Like, if you take Sunday, you're giving up the café shift, that's it. The bookstore was never going to happen that same second anyway. You compare it to one thing, not to everything stacked together."

Claire looked at her notebook. She crossed out the sum and wrote instead: café, then next to it, bookstore 50. If she took the Sunday shift, she was giving up seventy dollars, not seventy plus fifty. If she took the café, she was giving up whichever she'd actually have chosen second, and only that one. The math got smaller. It should have felt like relief, and for a second it did, a judicious little click, like simplifying an equation. Then Mahi said quietly, "It's still seventy dollars," and the relief tilted into something else, because the smaller number was still a real number, still a door with a real person behind it.

"I'll do Sunday," Claire told Kacey, before the feeling could turn into more arithmetic. "Tell Mr. Pham. And tell Marcus I'll miss it, or that I'm sending my apologies, or whatever people say." "Reparations," Kacey said solemnly. "You owe the poetry community reparation." "I owe the poetry community a coffee sometime," Claire said. Mahi raised her mug like a toast, and for a moment the three of them existed in the joke together, and the loss had edges you could laugh at.

She texted the café manager a polite no, and then, because it felt dishonest to let the bookstore imagine she was still deciding, she texted there too. She turned her chemistry back over and actually read a problem. The room was warm and the lamp buzzed faintly and Mahi had started narrating the contents of Claire's closet like a nature documentary, which never failed to captivate her, the voice low and faux-scientific, "and here we observe the species known as hoodie, in its natural habitat," when the phone rang again.

It was Mr. Pham. Claire put him on speaker, already smiling. "Claire. I'm so sorry. My sister is visiting from out of state, family matter, the nursery doesn't need Sunday help after all." She heard herself say, "Oh no, that's fine," while her eyes went to the notebook, to the seventy dollars she had counted and given up, the number she had made peace with. "You'll take me another weekend," he said, "of course, of course," and he was kind about it, and she thanked him and hung up.

"So," Mahi said, watching her from the closet, "do you call the café back?" Claire looked at the phone, at the two polite refusals she had already sent, at the chemistry problem she had solved without noticing, at the whole Sunday suddenly empty and bright and hers. "That's the funny part," she said. "I was so busy counting what I'd give up, I never counted what I was keeping." She picked up the phone and, for a long second, did not dial.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: A Riemann sum approximates the area under a curve by adding up the areas of thin rectangles, and the integral is the limit as the rectangles become infinitely thin.
story:
The summer before college, Hailey's grandmother kept the house at a temperature suited to someone raised without air conditioning, and Hailey had grown used to working at the kitchen table with a thin sheen of sweat on her forearms, her laptop open in front of the window fan. The placement exam was in three weeks. If she scored well, she could skip first-semester calculus; if she didn't, she would spend the fall on material she had already half-learned from videos at midnight, pausing and rewinding until the words lost shape.

Her grandmother set a glass of iced tea beside the laptop without asking, the way she set things down, as though the offering were the whole point and the object incidental. Hailey murmured thanks and stared again at the problem on her screen. Find the area under the curve y equals x squared, from zero to one. The textbook wanted her to do something with symbols, antiderivatives and bars, and the symbols moved when she looked at them, sliding apart like the parts of a sentence in a language she could pronounce but not yet read.

She texted Jayda, who had taken the class senior year and treated math the way other people treated gossip, as a system of who-did-what-to-whom. Jayda sent back a single line: stop trying to do it, start by guessing it. Hailey typed back that guessing felt like cheating, and Jayda replied with a photograph of her own notebook margin, where she had written rules are for people who already understand.

So Hailey guessed. She drew the curve on paper, then drew one rectangle under it, a single fat block from zero to one whose top corner touched the curve, and computed its area: one. Then she drew two rectangles, each half a unit wide, and added their areas: point one two five plus one, which came to one point one two five. It was too big. The rectangles' flat shoulders poked above the curve, and the overlap was the error, visible and almost insultingly simple. She drew four rectangles, then eight, and the total shrank each time, edging downward.

The grandmother came through with a dish towel over her shoulder and paused behind her long enough to read the screen. "You have made the window smaller," she said, nodding at the rectangles. Hailey said it wasn't a window, it was rectangles under a curve, and then heard herself and laughed. The grandmother patted her shoulder and said smaller pieces, truer picture, and went back to shelling peas on the porch, leaving Hailey with a sentence she hadn't asked for and couldn't shake.

She opened the spreadsheet her brother had left installed on the laptop and built it herself, column by column. Width in one cell, rectangle heights computed from the curve, a sum at the bottom. She set the width to one tenth and watched the total: one point three eight five. One hundredth: one point three three eight. One thousandth: one point three three three. The number was settling, the way the porch swing settled after you stopped pushing it, the last oscillations too small to see. She typed widths so tiny the spreadsheet had to display them in scientific notation, and the total stopped changing in any digit she could read.

She called Jayda anyway, phone wedged against her shoulder, because settling felt like something that should be witnessed. "It's converging," she said. "Like it wants to be a third."

"It always wants to be something," Jayda said, the television audible behind her, her attention split but kindly split. "Mr. Pierre used to call that a Riemann sum. Adding up the rectangles, then letting them get skinny forever."

"That has a name?"

"Everything you're discovering in June had a name by 1850. He said that too." Jayda's voice went briefly muffled, then returned. "He also said the integral is just the limit. Where the sum goes when the rectangles get infinitely thin."

Hailey wrote that down, then wrote it again underneath, differently, because the two versions weren't quite the same sentence and the difference was the thing she was chasing. The spreadsheet told her the area was a third, approximately, and the symbols in the textbook, when she worked them with fresh eyes, told her the area was exactly a third, and both were true, and neither alone was the whole truth. The approximation was how you believed it; the symbols were how you could promise it. She sat with that for a while, fanning herself with the notebook, unsure whether she had learned the idea or only its outline, unsure whether that distinction even mattered yet.

At dusk the grandmother called her to the porch, where the peas were done and the bowl of empty pods sat torpid in the heat, giving off their green smell. They ate cold noodles with peanuts because her grandmother was, in her own quiet way, an epicure of summer, believing that heat demanded specific foods and would not be argued with. Hailey ate slowly, and between bites she reached over and refilled her grandmother's glass from the sweating pitcher before her own, a small motion that earned her a look of pleased surprise, as if she had performed a trick.

Later, back at the table, she opened the spreadsheet one more time. She highlighted the column of widths and dragged it smaller, watching the total in the corner hold steady at one point three three three, and she thought of the curve and the rectangles beneath it growing countless and thin as wire. She closed the laptop halfway, leaving it breathing, and set her grandmother's empty glass in the sink.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
story:
Nicholas had rehearsed the greeting twice in the food court bathroom mirror, and both times the mirror had won. He smoothed his shirt front, exhumed from the back of his closet a collared thing his mother called his "grandpa casual" look, and walked toward the arcade entrance where Athena was supposed to meet him at two. Rylan had appointed himself tactical adviser on the grounds that he had been on one and a half dates, the half being a group project that got emotional.

"Rule one," Rylan had said that morning, texting from the sabbatical his parents had imposed on his phone, meaning he could only use the kitchen tablet after dinner. "Don't plan anything scary. Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement gets mistaken for attraction to the person nearby. So no haunted house, no cliff jumping, nothing with a drop."

"That's the least romantic advice I've ever heard."

"It's science. You want a boring date. Boring lets the real feelings show up on time."

Nicholas had laughed at him, but now, standing under the mall's flickering skylight, he found himself steering Athena toward the safest option in the building, the candle shop, where nothing moved and everything smelled like a grandmother's memory of a beach. Athena, who had spent the walk describing her plan to be impecunious and proud of it during a gap year, stopped dead at the threshold.

"We're not going to smell candles for an hour," she said. "I came to do something. There's a bowling alley downstairs and I have a rivalry to settle."

"You have a rivalry with me? We've known each other since September."

"Exactly. Nine months of unresolved competition." She was already walking. He followed, and his heart, which had been behaving with reasonable dignity near the candles, began hammering on the escalator down.

The alley was loud and blue-lit, and by the fourth frame Nicholas had discovered he was terrible in a way that seemed almost deliberate, like his body had unionized against him. Athena was good, casually, infuriatingly good, narrating her own follow-through like a golf announcer. Then she suggested a tiebreaker, one frame each, winner picks where they ate. Her first ball left her a seven-ten split and she converted it with a scream of triumph that turned heads three lanes over. Nicholas needed a strike to tie. He stood at the line, ball sweating in his palms, and his heart was going so hard he could see his sleeve move.

He rolled, and knocked down eight. He turned around laughing, and there she was, delighted, already declaring her prize, and his chest was still buzzing, and he honestly could not tell what the buzzing was. Fear of the tenth pin? Joy at losing to her? The other thing? He thought of Rylan's rule and its fatal flaw: the science told you the signal could be crossed, but not which way it was crossed. A garbled message doesn't come with a decoder ring.

"Your hands were shaking," Athena said, handing him his shoes. "Was it the pressure, or do you always shake around me?"

"That's a diagnostic question."

"I'm a diagnostic person." She laced her shoes without looking up, which he understood was mercy. "For the record, mine's both. Probably. I haven't finished the experiment either."

Nicholas considered telling her about misattribution, the whole borrowed framework of it, and decided to hold it back like a card he hadn't learned to play. Instead he picked up the ball one more time, rolled it dead straight down the empty lane, and watched every pin go down at last, all ten, for nobody's score.

"Overtime," Athena said, and wrote her initials on the scoreboard screen.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
The phone repair shop smelled of isopropyl alcohol and the dour patience of customers waiting on dead screens, and Parker had spent every Saturday behind the counter since September, learning to pry open other people's lives with a suction cup and a guitar pick. His boss, the owner, had gone to the bank, leaving him alone with the register and a queue of three, when Sterling pushed through the door holding his phone out like a verdict.

"You have to see this before it blows up," Sterling said, though it was already blowing up, the numbers under the photo climbing in the way that made his voice thin and quick. The image showed a flooded street, brown water to the door handles, a man on a roof holding a handwritten sign. "Riverbend this morning. Sixty thousand shares in two hours. If I post it to the school accounts right now, before the news picks it up, everyone's going to come through me first." That was what Sterling wanted; he'd said it plainly enough before, that being first was its own recompense, that speed was the only currency the internet actually paid out.

Parker set down the cracked iPad he'd been working on. The photo was sharp, well-framed, and something about that bothered him before he could say why. Maybe it was that disasters were rarely so composed. Or maybe it was Ms. Shapiro, the retired teacher from two doors down, who came in every Saturday to have him back up her photos and who had once told him, while he coaxed her contacts off a water-damaged phone, that a picture without a date was a rumor wearing a costume.

"I don't know," Parker said.

"You don't know what? It's a photo."

"That's what I don't know." He turned the loaner laptop toward himself and, half remembering something Ms. Shapiro had shown him when they'd hunted down a picture of her old classroom, typed the name of the site she used: TinEye. She'd called it a reverse image search, and she liked it, she said, because it was launched in 2008, before everybody decided that looking things up was too much trouble. He dragged Sterling's photo into the search bar and they both watched the little wheel turn.

The results loaded slowly, one after another, and Parker noticed the sort option at the top of the page and switched it to oldest first, because if the picture were really from this morning, the oldest result would still be this morning. The wheel turned again. The oldest result was not this morning. It was not even this year. The same photo, the same man on the same roof with the same sign, had appeared online years before, in a flood that happened somewhere else entirely, and every share since then was just the same water rising again in a new feed.

Sterling's shoulders dropped. He looked at the climbing number under his repost of it, which had already passed four hundred, and then at the screen, and Parker understood that what his friend was deciding in that silence was whether the numbers still counted if the photo was a ghost. "It's still a real flood somewhere," Sterling said, which was true in a way that desiccated the moment you held it up, because it was not this flood, not this river, not this morning, and the man on the roof had been rescued years ago by people who had long since forgotten him.

"It's real somewhere," Parker said. "Just not where we said it was."

Sterling deleted his post, then sat with his thumbs hovering, wanting to be the one to expose the fake, which Parker could see was the same hunger wearing a better shirt. Behind them the bell over the door chimed, and Ms. Shapiro came in with her tablet under her arm and her reading glasses pushed up into her hair. She glanced at the laptop, at the column of dates descending into the past, and raised one eyebrow at Parker.

"Oldest first," she said.

"Oldest first," he agreed, and pulled a stool over for her at the counter.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: The first known mention of binary search in computing was by John Mauchly in 1946, in the Moore School Lectures, an early course on electronic computers.
story:
The timeline went up on the wall of the computer lab the way everything in Ms. Popescu's coding club went up: slightly crooked, taped at the corners, subject to revision. It was a long sheet of butcher paper with dates and names, Euclid near one end, and the argument had started before Nicole finished unzipping her backpack.

"Binary search is ancient," Devon was saying, tapping the paper. "People have been splitting dictionaries in half forever."

"That's not the same as writing it down for a machine," Romane said. "The timeline is about computing."

Nicole pulled out her laptop and opened the file she'd been avoiding all week. Her search assignment was due at the end of the meeting: implement a linear search, implement a binary search, and explain to the room why one beat the other on sorted data. She had the code half working. The explaining was the part that scared her.

"Fine," Devon said. "Then find when it was first mentioned for computers. Actually find it, don't just say it."

Ms. Popescu, who had been watering the sad spider plant by the window, turned around with the watering can still in her hand. "That's a good question. Whoever answers it gets to add the card to the timeline."

Nicole watched Romane and Devon both reach for their phones, and felt the small competitive pull herself. But she had a deadline. She typed `def linear_search` and let the argument continue behind her, a low argumentative weather system moving through the room.

Her linear search worked on the first try, which felt like a platitude of programming: the simple thing always runs, and the simple thing is always the one you have to apologize for. She wrote the loop, tested it against a list of two hundred sorted names, and timed it. Then she opened a fresh file for binary search and stalled. She knew the shape of it, halving and halving again, but her fingers kept wanting to write the loop she already trusted.

"Nicole." Romane dropped into the chair beside her, phone screen up. "Look at this. John Mauchly. The first known mention of binary search in computing was by him, in 1946, in the Moore School Lectures."

"Which were what?"

"An early course on electronic computers. That's all I've got so far."

"Mauchly," Devon said from across the room, in the tone of someone conceding a point he intended to keep fighting anyway. "That's the ENIAC guy. So it's 1946 on the wall. Write the card."

Romane wrote it. Nicole copied the sentence into her notes file, because the assignment asked for context, and context was the thing she'd been planning to fake. She went back to the binary search, and this time, instead of trying to hold the whole algorithm in her head, she did what she did in English class: she read her own linear search like a text and asked what it was wasting. It read every element. Every single one, front to back, like checking every locker in a hallway when the lockers are alphabetized and you know the alphabet. A sorted list was a promise, and the linear search ignored the promise. The binary search was what happened when you kept the promise in mind: look in the middle, and half the hallway disappears.

She typed it in fifteen lines. Tested it. The timer said something so much smaller than the linear search's number that she ran both again, certain she'd made an error. She hadn't.

When it was her turn at the front, she stood with her laptop facing the group and the timeline behind her, Mauchly's card freshly taped at 1946. Devon had gone quiet, which for Devon was a kind of applause.

"Linear search checks every item in order," she said. "Binary search checks the middle, and because the data is sorted, it can throw away half the remaining items every step. Two hundred sorted names, and it needs at most eight checks." She paused. "But it only works because of the sort. On unsorted data, halving tells you nothing, and you'd be back to reading every locker anyway."

Ms. Popescu raised a hand, not to interrupt but the way she did when she wanted a student to slow down and land a point. "And if the data changes constantly?"

"Then keeping it sorted might cost more than the search saves," Nicole said. "I don't actually know where the line is. I know binary search wins on sorted data. I don't know how often real data stays sorted enough for it to matter."

The admission sat in the room for a second, and Romane nodded slowly, as though the not-knowing were part of the answer rather than a hole in it. Devon exhumed his phone from under a tangle of earbuds and started typing, presumably to verify the Mauchly date again, but after a moment he put it face down on the table.

After the meeting, Nicole stayed to help Ms. Popescu take down the chairs. The coach from the robotics team came by to borrow the projector, choleric as always about the settings, and Ms. Popescu talked him down without any of it turning into a real fight.

Nicole looked at the timeline before leaving. Mauchly, 1946, Moore School Lectures, taped beside a card someone had just added in green marker. She still didn't know where the line was between sorted and unsorted lives, but she knew how to stand in front of a room and say so.

"Same time next week?" Romane called from the doorway, holding it open with her hip.

"Bring the list of names," Nicole said. "I want to watch it halve again."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder the youngest child present customarily asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah, beginning with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
The power on Maple Street had been out since noon, and by five o'clock Addison's mother had surrendered the kitchen entirely, piling the Seder plates into laundry baskets and directing everyone toward the park pavilion at the end of the block. Addison carried the Haggadot in a canvas bag against her hip, the same worn paperback copies her grandmother had used, and behind her walked Kaylee and Chanel, who had texted her that morning asking if they could come. They had never been to a Seder. Addison had said yes before she thought about what yes would require of her.

The pavilion smelled of charcoal from somebody else's cookout and of the early April mud, and Ms. Patel from two doors down was already there, helping her mother unfold the folding tables. Ms. Patel had brought a tray of spiced nuts and stayed to watch, saying that the park in spring was practically its own biome, everything green and damp and teeming. The candles went into mason jars because the wind kept finding the flame. Addison set the Seder plate down carefully, turning the shank bone toward the center of the table the way her grandmother used to, and felt the evening arrange itself around her like something she could either hold or drop.

She had been practicing for two weeks. The Hebrew was not the difficulty; she had chanted it in the shower, on the bus, once under her breath during a calculus quiz she had already finished. What she wanted, though she hadn't said it that way even to herself, was to be the one asking the Four Questions this year, the way she had at seven, at eight, at nine, small and terrified and then suddenly lit up from the inside when the whole table turned toward her voice. She was the youngest in her immediate family. She had assumed the custom followed her the way a shadow does.

Then her uncle's car pulled into the lot, and out climbed her little cousin, seven years old, gap where his front teeth had been, gripping a stick he had found somewhere and refusing to relinquish it even for the seating chart. Addison watched him take the chair beside his father and felt the assumption rearrange itself, quietly and without ceremony. The youngest child present. That was the whole of it. She looked at the Haggadot in her bag and understood that of course the questions had never been hers to keep, only hers to pass along.

"Wait," Chanel whispered, leaning close while the adults poured the first cups. "So there's a script? Nobody's going to just talk?" Addison kept her voice low, aware of her mother arranging matzah into its cloth sleeve three feet away. "There's an order to the whole night, and early on, the youngest kid here asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah. It starts with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'" Kaylee nodded slowly, the way she did when she was filing something away. "And that's him," she said, tilting her chin toward the cousin, who was now attempting to balance the stick vertically on the table. "That's him," Addison said.

She slid her chair around the corner of the table before she could decide against it. Her cousin looked up with the flat suspicion of a seven-year-old who has been ambushed at family events before. "You know the part you're doing tonight?" she asked. He shook his head, and the stick toppled. "It's the best part," she said. "Everyone at the table has to listen to you and only you. I did it for years." He considered this. "Is it long?" "Four questions. I'll say the first words with you, then you take over. If you get stuck, I'm right there." He studied her face for whatever seven-year-olds study faces for, and then he nodded, once, judicious as a judge, and let her take the stick and set it on the bench behind them.

They ran it twice in the fading light, her whispering the opening line and him catching the melody on the second phrase, stumbling on the third, getting it on the fourth. Ms. Patel offered a judicious amount of applause when he finished the second run, and he pretended not to enjoy it while his whole body contradicted him. Whether he would hold together under the actual candles, under forty eyes instead of two, Addison could not know, and she noticed that she did not mind not knowing. She had wanted the questions for herself, and instead she had gotten something she could not have parametrized on any graph: the exact shape of the moment handing itself forward.

When the candles were lit and her father lifted the first cup, the pavilion went quiet except for the wind moving in the maples behind them. Her cousin stood up, and Addison saw his hands shake, and she leaned toward him and gave him the first words in a breath he alone could hear. "Why," he began, his voice cracking upward, "is this night different from all other nights?"

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Binary search needs to jump straight to the middle item, so it loses its advantage on a linked list, where reaching the middle means walking through the items one by one.
story:
Addison had never once missed a deadline in Mr. Tan's computer science class, and she did not intend to start with the search assignment, which was due Thursday and which she had, of course, already finished. Mostly finished. The part she had finished was the explanation: binary search beats linear search on sorted data because you jump to the middle item, compare, and throw away half the list every time, instead of checking items one by one. She could say that in her sleep. The part she had mostly finished was the code.

She stayed after the bell in the lab, because the lab had better chairs and because Erica would be at track until six. George was already there, leaning over his laptop with the concentration of someone defending a castle. "Don't talk to me," he said. "I'm losing to my own program."

"Mine works," Addison said, which was true in the sense that it ran. She had built her data as a linked list, because that was what Tuesday's lesson had covered and she liked doing things in order, and she had bolted her binary search on top of it. She ran it again on a list of ten thousand names and watched the counter at the bottom of the screen. She ran her old linear search on the same list. The counters came out nearly identical. She sat very still, the way you do when you suspect the problem is you.

"That can't be right," she said. "Binary search is supposed to be fast. Half, then half, then half."

George looked over without asking permission. "You put it on a linked list?"

"Obviously. That's what we just learned."

"Yeah, but binary search needs to jump straight to the middle item." He tapped her screen, once, above her search function. "Look at what you wrote to get there."

She looked. Her function, when it needed the middle of the list, walked there. Item by item, following pointers from the head, counting as it went, exactly what a linear search did. So every "fast" step of her clever algorithm began with a slow crawl. She had written the crawl herself, three days ago, and had felt quite pleased about it at the time.

"Fine," she said, because admitting things outright was not something she did in front of George. "I'll compartmentalize it. Data structure over here, algorithm over there." She drew two boxes in her notebook, which is what she did when a problem was behaving badly. But the boxes didn't help, because the problem lived in the gap between them. The algorithm's speed assumed the structure could jump. Hers couldn't. She wrote in the margin: the advantage isn't in the idea alone, it's in the idea plus what the structure allows. Then she crossed out "allow" and wrote "afford," then felt pretentious and crossed that out too.

When Erica came in, still in her warmups, hair damp, she dropped her bag on the table and read the margin upside down. "You're doing philosophy in a coding class now?"

"It's not philosophy. It's just that I was wrong."

"Okay, who are you and what have you done with Addison." Erica pulled out a chair. "You're never wrong. You're the person who told the whole class the student council was an oligarchy and got Mr. Tan to put it on a quiz."

"That was a different subject. And I was mostly joking." She hadn't been joking. She'd also, she could admit to herself if not to Erica, been showing off, the way she'd shown off the linked list code she'd been so proud of, code that had quietly ruined the thing built on top of it. She was starting to suspect she did that. She wasn't sure what to do with the suspicion, so she set it next to the notebook, unfinished.

Mr. Tan came by on his way out, keys already in hand. "How's the search going, Addison?"

"Binary search doesn't beat linear search," she said, and then, before he could answer, "on a linked list. Because getting to the middle means walking through the items one by one. So it's the same speed. Or close."

He didn't correct her, which she took as a kind of trophy. "So what are you going to do about it?" he said, and left before she could give the answer she didn't have yet.

She started deleting her walk-to-the-middle function. The cursor blinked at the end of the line, and outside the window the late light came through the branches of the big elm at an angle that made the tree look almost arboreal in silhouette, black and splitting against the orange sky, and she thought, absurdly, that the root was on the wrong side. George closed his laptop. "Dinner," he said. "You coming?"

"In a minute," she said, and typed `array[0]` at the top of a fresh file.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
The office smelled of toner and someone's microwaved soup, and Cohen had been sitting in the chair by the window for forty minutes while his mother finished a call that kept almost ending. He had come in to drop off her lunch, the container sweating through the paper bag, and then the call had started, and now he was watching the parking lot fill with cars whose drivers looked like they all had somewhere better to be.

His phone buzzed. Leanna had sent a video with the caption "look at this, we HAVE to share this, it's insane." It showed a flooded street, water to the door handles, a man carrying a child on his shoulders past a submerged bus. Text over the footage said it had been recorded that morning, three towns over, and that the city had done nothing to warn anyone. Underneath, a comment thread was already furious, hundreds of people promising to make someone answer for it.

Cohen watched it twice. The water was brown and fast, the child's sneaker dangling off one foot, and it did look insane. His thumb was already over the share button when Louis-Thomas texted a separate message: "before you repost that flood thing, run SIFT on it. You said you didn't know it yet, so, quick version." Then, in pieces, the way Louis-Thomas always typed: "it's from Mike Caulfield, an educator." "Stop. Investigate the source. Find better coverage. Trace claims to their original context." "that's what the letters stand for. do the S first."

Stop. Cohen set the phone on his knee, screen dark, and looked out at the parking lot again. A woman in a mustard coat was helping an older man unload a box from his trunk, holding the door with her hip. His mother was still on the call; he could hear her say "no, that's fair" in the voice she used when she was agreeing to something she disliked. The not-sharing sat in his hand like a held breath.

Investigate the source. The account that had posted the video had a name like a news outlet with two letters moved around, and when he opened its page, everything on it was floods, fires, and politicians' faces with red circles drawn on them. Nothing was dated. Nothing linked anywhere. He thought of a kid in his civics class who had once argued that speed mattered more than accuracy because attention was the only real currency now, and Cohen had nodded along, and he hadn't liked himself for the nodding. He realized he'd been a sycophant for the argument, agreeing because it was easier than holding his ground.

He needed better coverage, so he tried the thing Louis-Thomas had mentioned weeks ago and Cohen had half ignored: a reverse image search. He paused the video on the clearest frame, the man and the child and the bus, and fed it into the search. The results loaded slowly on the office's guest wifi, and while they did, a woman came out of the conference room and asked if he wanted water. Ms. Delgado, his mother's colleague, the one who had given him a biology textbook when he was fourteen. He said yes, thank you, and she brought a paper cup filled to the brim, careful not to spill it on the desk.

The results came up. The same frame, the same man, the same child with the sneaker hanging. But the pages were old. The image had appeared two years before, attached to flooding in a different country entirely, and one news article traced it back further still, to a photographer's portfolio with a date and a place and a caption that named the man as a volunteer, not a stranded resident. The video's claimed context, the text about that morning and three towns over, was a costume draped over an old body.

Trace the claim to its original context. He had, or near enough. He sat with that for a moment, aware of two feelings that refused to merge. One was certainty: the post was false, and sharing it would have made him a small part of a machine that manufactured anger out of stolen images. The other was uneasiness, harder to name. Leanna had shared it because she cared about the child on the man's shoulders; the caring was real even if the image was not, and floods like that one did happen, somewhere, to somebody. Refusing the share was right, but it didn't feel like a victory over anything. It felt like the honest half of a larger job.

He texted Leanna back the link to the photographer's page, then typed and deleted three different explanations, each one sounding more like a lecture than the last. Finally he wrote: "it's from two years ago, different country. here's the original. the anger's still fair, just aim it somewhere real." He thought about the difference between that and silence, between correcting and condescending, and he didn't fully know where the line was. Some obdurate part of him still wanted to just repost it anyway, because three hundred comments meant three hundred people who already agreed with him, and that warmth was seductive in a way he understood and distrusted.

His mother finally hung up and came over, apologizing with her whole face before her mouth caught up. She asked what he'd been doing all that time, and he started to say "nothing," the automatic answer, and then stopped. He showed her the two images side by side on his phone, the viral one and the original, and watched her squint and tilt her head. "That's the same kid," she said slowly. "It is," Cohen said. Ms. Delgado leaned over from her desk, drawn by the two of them bent over the screen, and Cohen slid the phone toward her so she could see.

"It's called SIFT," he said. "Stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, trace claims to their original context." Ms. Delgado pulled her chair closer and tapped the photographer's page with one finger, and his mother said she was going to forward it to her sister, who had already posted the video twice.
